q.q: Consumer confidence rises while firms become more pessimistic about future sales. What can be concluded about aggregate demand?
options: Consumption and investment both tend to rise; both changes shift AD right
Consumption and investment both tend to fall; both changes shift AD left
Consumption tends to rise and investment to fall; the two changes cancel because they oppose
Consumption tends to rise and investment to fall; relative changes determine the net shift
q.commonError: Letting one shifter determine the combined result.
q.feedback: Confidence raises consumption, while pessimism lowers investment; magnitudes determine the net shift.

q.q: The price level falls, but taxes rise at the same time. Which statement is most precise?
options: Both changes cause movement along AD.
The price-level change shifts AD right and the tax increase shifts AD left.
The price-level change causes movement along AD, while the tax increase shifts AD left.
Both changes shift AD left.
q.commonError: Confusing a change in the price level with a nonprice AD shifter.
q.feedback: The price level is on the graph’s vertical axis; taxes are an external shifter.

q.q: Foreign income falls sharply while domestic firms increase investment. The effect on domestic aggregate demand is:
options: A certain rightward shift
A certain leftward shift
Ambiguous because net exports fall while investment rises.
A movement upward along AD
q.commonError: Ignoring offsetting components of aggregate demand.
q.feedback: Lower foreign income reduces exports, while higher investment raises AD.

q.q: A higher price level increases money demand, which raises interest rates and reduces investment. This sequence explains:
options: A rightward shift of LRAS
A rightward shift of AD
A leftward shift of SRAS
A movement upward and leftward along the existing AD curve.
q.commonError: Treating the interest-rate effect as a shift of AD.
q.feedback: The interest-rate effect is one reason quantity of real GDP demanded falls as the price level rises.

q.q: The price level rises at the same time that the government cuts taxes. Which graph description is correct?
options: The price rise shifts AD left; the tax cut moves downward along that curve
The price rise moves upward along AD; the tax cut shifts AD right
The price rise moves downward along AD; the tax cut shifts AD right
The price rise moves upward along AD; the tax cut shifts AD left
q.commonError: Treating simultaneous movement and shift as mutually exclusive.
q.feedback: The price-level change causes movement along AD; the tax cut shifts the curve.

q.q: Domestic interest rates fall because the central bank expands money supply, while foreign income also falls. What can be said about AD?
options: Investment rises and export demand falls; the net AD direction requires their relative effects
Investment falls and export demand falls; both changes push AD left
Investment rises and export demand rises; both changes push AD right
Investment rises and export demand falls; equal numbers of opposing channels imply no AD shift
q.commonError: Ignoring offsetting investment and net-export effects.
q.feedback: The two shifters push different AD components in opposite directions.

q.q: A student says, “Any fall in real GDP means AD shifted left.” What is the best correction?
options: A fall in output could reflect AD shifting left or SRAS shifting right; price and shock evidence is needed
A fall in output could reflect AD shifting right or SRAS shifting left; price and shock evidence is needed
A fall in output could reflect only movement down AD; price and shock evidence is needed
A fall in output could reflect AD shifting left, SRAS shifting left, or movement up AD; price and shock evidence is needed
q.commonError: Inferring a curve shift from an outcome without identifying the cause.
q.feedback: Observed output changes do not by themselves reveal which curve moved.

q.q: The government cuts taxes while the central bank raises interest rates. What is the strongest conclusion about aggregate demand?
options: The net shift is uncertain because the policies oppose each other.
Aggregate demand must rise because tax cuts always dominate.
Aggregate demand must fall because interest rates always dominate.
Both policies reduce consumption and investment.
q.commonError: Declaring a definite aggregate-demand result without comparing opposing policy effects.
q.feedback: The tax cut supports consumption, while higher interest rates restrain investment and durable spending; relative magnitudes determine the net shift.

q.q: A tax increase and higher government purchases occur together. Which statement is justified without numerical information?
options: The two policies push aggregate demand in opposite directions.
AD must shift left
The policies cause only movement along AD
AD must shift right
q.commonError: Assuming a combined policy has a predetermined net effect.
q.feedback: Higher G raises AD; higher taxes tend to reduce consumption and AD.

q.q: A country’s currency appreciates and foreign economies enter recession while domestic consumer confidence rises. The net AD effect is:
options: Left: consumption and net exports both fall
Right: consumption and net exports both rise
Ambiguous: consumption rises while net exports fall
Unchanged: higher consumption exactly offsets lower net exports
q.commonError: Assuming offsetting forces are equal without evidence.
q.feedback: Confidence raises C, while appreciation and lower foreign income reduce NX.

q.q: The price level falls while firms cut investment. What occurs?
options: Only movement upward along AD
Only a rightward AD shift
Movement downward along AD plus a leftward AD shift.
A rightward SRAS shift only
q.commonError: Failing to separate price-level movement from a spending shift.
q.feedback: The lower price level changes quantity demanded; lower investment shifts AD left.

q.q: Consumer confidence rises and the currency appreciates. The net AD direction is:
options: No change because the effects are equal
Ambiguous because consumption rises while net exports fall.
Certainly rightward
Certainly leftward
q.commonError: Assuming offsetting shifters cancel exactly.
q.feedback: The two components move in opposite directions, and magnitudes matter.

q.q: Why does leverage make banks riskier?
options: A small percentage loss on assets can wipe out a large share of capital.
It guarantees assets never fall in value.
It prevents banks from making loans.
It makes reserves unnecessary.
q.commonError: thinking leverage only increases returns and not risk
q.feedback: Leverage magnifies gains and losses. A small asset loss can hit capital hard.

q.q: If excess reserves are $25,000, actual reserves are $85,000, and the reserve ratio is 12 percent, what are deposits?
q.commonError: forgetting to find required reserves before solving deposits
q.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $85,000 - $25,000 = $60,000. Deposits = $60,000 / 0.12 = $500,000.

q.q: A bank has actual reserves of $96,000, excess reserves of $24,000, and a reserve requirement of 12 percent. What are deposits?
q.commonError: dividing actual reserves by the reserve ratio instead of required reserves
q.feedback: Required reserves are actual minus excess: $96,000 - $24,000 = $72,000. Deposits are $72,000 / 0.12 = $600,000.

q.q: A bank has $2 million in assets and $100,000 in capital. If asset values fall by 5 percent, what happens to capital?
options: It falls to zero.
It falls by $5,000.
It rises to $200,000.
It stays at $100,000.
q.commonError: applying the percentage loss to capital instead of assets
q.feedback: Five percent of $2 million is $100,000. That wipes out the bank's $100,000 in capital.

q.q: A price ceiling is set above equilibrium. Why does it usually have no effect?
options: The market price remains below the legal maximum
Because all price ceilings create shortages
Because sellers are forced to charge the maximum
Because quantity supplied must equal zero
q.commonError: thinks_legal_maximum_must_be_actual_price
q.feedback: A nonbinding ceiling is above equilibrium, so the market can still reach equilibrium below the legal maximum.

q.q: A rent ceiling lowers the money rent but causes long search times, side payments, and poorer maintenance. What is the best interpretation?
options: Lower legal rent can be offset by nonmoney costs.
The ceiling eliminated scarcity
The ceiling created a surplus of apartments
The price ceiling shifted demand left
q.commonError: ignores_nonmoney_costs_under_shortage
q.feedback: A binding ceiling can lower the legal price but create search costs, rationing, and quality decline.

q.q: A legal maximum price is set above equilibrium. A student predicts a shortage. What is wrong?
options: A ceiling above equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a shortage
Any price ceiling always creates a shortage
A ceiling above equilibrium creates a surplus
A ceiling above equilibrium is actually a price floor
q.commonError: thinks_all_ceilings_bind
q.feedback: A price ceiling binds only when it is below equilibrium.

q.q: A binding price ceiling on gasoline leads stations to sell out early. Some stations favor regular customers. What is the best interpretation?
options: The shortage creates nonprice rationing
The market clears because the legal price is low
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling increases supply
q.commonError: thinks_low_legal_price_solves_scarcity
q.feedback: When price cannot ration the good, other methods like waiting, favoritism, and side payments can take over.

q.q: A rent ceiling causes landlords to convert apartments into short-term rentals outside the regulated market. What does this show?
options: The ceiling reduced regulated rental supply by changing landlord incentives.
A ceiling always increases quantity supplied
A ceiling eliminates opportunity cost for landlords
A ceiling is nonbinding if landlords find loopholes
q.commonError: assumes_legal_price_change_does_not_affect_supplier_behavior
q.feedback: A binding ceiling lowers returns in the regulated market and can push suppliers to adjust around the policy.

q.q: A city subsidizes apartment construction while also imposing a binding rent ceiling. Which combined result is most likely?
options: More supply can ease—but not necessarily end—rationing under a binding ceiling.
The subsidy makes the ceiling irrelevant in all cases
The ceiling shifts demand left and eliminates scarcity
The policy must create a surplus because supply increases
q.commonError: assumes_one_policy_fully_cancels_the_other
q.feedback: A supply subsidy can ease shortage pressure, but a binding ceiling can still hold price below equilibrium and cause rationing.

q.q: A price floor is set below equilibrium. Why does it usually have no effect?
options: The market price remains above the legal minimum
Because all price floors create surpluses
Because buyers must pay the legal minimum even if equilibrium is higher
Because quantity demanded must equal zero
q.commonError: thinks_legal_minimum_must_be_actual_price
q.feedback: A nonbinding floor is below equilibrium, so the market can still reach equilibrium above the legal minimum.

q.q: A legal minimum price is set below equilibrium. A student predicts a surplus. What is wrong?
options: A floor below equilibrium is nonbinding and does not create a surplus
Any price floor always creates a surplus
A floor below equilibrium creates a shortage
A floor below equilibrium is actually a price ceiling
q.commonError: thinks_all_floors_bind
q.feedback: A price floor binds only when it is above equilibrium.

q.q: A binding price floor on milk leaves producers with unsold inventory. Which hidden cost is most likely?
options: Waste, storage costs, or government purchases to support the price
Long lines among buyers because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Black-market premiums from buyers competing for scarce milk
No cost because producers receive a higher legal price
q.commonError: ignores_costs_of_surplus
q.feedback: A binding floor creates a surplus, which can lead to waste, storage costs, or policy costs.

q.q: A minimum wage is set above equilibrium, but employment does not fall much. Which explanation best fits supply and demand logic?
options: Labor demand may be relatively inelastic over that range
The law of demand has been disproven
The wage floor must be below equilibrium
Higher wages always increase quantity demanded for labor
q.commonError: expects_large_quantity_change_from_every_price_change
q.feedback: If labor demand is relatively inelastic, employment may fall only modestly when wages rise.

q.q: The government sets a crop price floor above equilibrium and promises to buy any unsold output. Which result is most likely?
options: Farmers produce more than consumers buy, so the government purchases and stores the surplus
Consumers buy more because the legal price is higher
The policy creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
The floor is nonbinding because the government participates in the market
q.commonError: confuses_government_purchase_with_market_clearing
q.feedback: A binding price floor creates excess supply. A purchase guarantee shifts the unsold surplus to the government rather than making it disappear.

q.q: A binding agricultural price floor is removed. Holding other conditions constant, which adjustment is expected?
options: Price rises, quantity demanded falls, and quantity supplied rises
Price falls, quantity demanded rises, and quantity supplied falls
Price and quantity supplied both rise
A shortage necessarily replaces the surplus
q.commonError: ignores_quantity_demanded_response
q.feedback: Removing the floor allows price to fall toward equilibrium, raising demand and reducing supply.

q.q: The domestic real interest rate rises, but political risk also rises sharply. What can be concluded about NCO?
options: NCO rises because risk determines flows independently of returns
NCO is unchanged because NX = NCO forces the channels to cancel
The direction is ambiguous because the two forces push NCO oppositely
NCO falls because interest returns determine flows independently of risk
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “NCO rises because risk determines flows independently of returns” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
q.feedback: Higher domestic returns tend to lower NCO, while greater domestic risk tends to raise it; relative magnitudes are needed.

q.q: Why does a higher domestic real interest rate lower NCO rather than raise it in the standard model?
options: It makes foreign assets relatively more attractive to domestic savers
It raises outward investment by increasing the return on foreign bonds
It favors domestic assets over foreign assets for both domestic and foreign investors
It attracts foreign funds that enter positively in the definition of NCO
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It makes foreign assets relatively more attractive to domestic savers” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
q.feedback: The relative-return change keeps more domestic funds at home and attracts more foreign funds.

q.q: Gross capital outflows rise while NCO falls. Which change can explain both facts?
options: The trade balance becomes unrelated to NCO
Gross capital inflows rise by more than gross outflows
Gross inflows fall by the same amount
Domestic purchases of foreign assets become zero
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The trade balance becomes unrelated to NCO” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
q.feedback: NCO is a net measure; it can fall despite larger outflows if foreign purchases of domestic assets rise even more.

q.q: Political instability raises desired foreign-asset purchases, and the domestic real interest rate rises in response. How should the second effect be interpreted?
options: The higher rate reinforces NCO by making foreign assets more attractive
The rate converts the capital outflow into domestic investment
The rate leaves NCO unchanged because capital flight is permanent
The higher rate partly restrains the initial increase in NCO
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The higher rate reinforces NCO by making foreign assets more attractive” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
q.feedback: Capital flight shifts desired NCO outward, while the higher domestic return produces movement toward domestic assets along the new relationship.

q.q: Domestic rates rise 2 percentage points, foreign rates rise 3 points, and domestic political risk falls. What can be inferred about NCO?
options: Foreign returns rise relative to domestic returns, raising NCO, and lower domestic risk also raises it; NCO rises
Foreign returns rise relative to domestic returns, raising NCO, while lower domestic risk reduces it; the opposing channels exactly cancel
Foreign returns rise relative to domestic returns, raising NCO, while lower domestic risk reduces it; the net direction is undetermined
Domestic returns rise relative to foreign returns, reducing NCO, and lower domestic risk also reduces it; NCO falls
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Foreign returns rise relative to domestic returns, raising NCO, and lower domestic risk also raises it; NCO rises” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
q.feedback: Foreign returns rise one point relative to domestic returns, tending to raise NCO, while safer domestic assets tend to lower it; magnitudes decide the net effect.

q.q: Domestic rates rise while foreign risk also rises. What is the likely combined effect on domestic NCO?
options: The effects necessarily cancel
Both changes tend to reduce it
Both changes tend to increase it
The rate raises it while foreign risk lowers it
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The rate raises it while foreign risk lowers it” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
q.feedback: Higher domestic returns favor home assets, and riskier foreign assets further discourage purchases abroad.

q.q: The domestic real interest rate rises and NCO falls. How does this change reach the foreign-exchange market?
options: A lower NCO raises demand for domestic currency
A higher rate makes foreign-exchange supply horizontal
NCO affects only goods markets
A lower NCO reduces the supply of domestic currency
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A lower NCO raises demand for domestic currency” in this capital flows and net capital outflow task.
q.feedback: With fewer net foreign-asset purchases, residents exchange less domestic currency for foreign currency, so FX supply shifts left.

q.q: Which institutional arrangement best combines central-bank independence with democratic accountability?
options: Public officials set the mandate; the central bank chooses instruments and reports transparently.
The central bank chooses national goals and never explains its decisions to the public.
Elected officials directly set policy interest rates before every national election.
The Treasury secretly directs monetary operations without a published mandate.
q.commonError: Treating independence as freedom from any public mandate or oversight.
q.feedback: Instrument independence can coexist with a legislated mandate, transparency, and public accountability.

q.q: When the central bank buys a large quantity of longer-term securities, what happens directly on its balance sheet?
options: Tax revenue rises while currency liabilities disappear from the balance sheet.
Its securities assets and reserve liabilities usually both rise.
Government purchases of goods rise automatically with the securities purchase.
Commercial-bank capital is converted directly into federal tax receipts.
q.commonError: Treating asset purchases as ordinary fiscal spending.
q.feedback: A central-bank asset purchase expands its asset holdings and typically creates reserve liabilities.

q.q: The short-term policy rate is near its effective lower bound. Which action is still a monetary-policy option?
options: Change federal income-tax rates through the banking system.
Authorize a new congressional spending program immediately.
Use forward guidance or buy longer-term securities.
Set private-sector wages and prices by administrative order.
q.commonError: Assuming monetary policy has no remaining tools when a short-term rate is very low.
q.feedback: Central banks may use communication and balance-sheet tools when conventional rate cuts are constrained.

q.q: A central-bank asset purchase sharply increases reserve balances, yet commercial-bank lending changes little. Which statement best separates the institutions’ roles?
options: The central bank failed to create any reserve balances because commercial banks did not expand loans after the asset purchase
Commercial banks create central-bank reserves whenever they choose not to lend
Reserve balances are identical to bank capital, so unchanged lending proves capital was unchanged
The central bank creates reserves; commercial-bank deposit creation still depends on lending and borrowing
q.commonError: Assumes that creating reserves automatically forces commercial banks to make loans and expand deposits.
q.feedback: The central bank can supply reserves, but broad deposit creation also depends on banks, borrowers, and redepositing behavior.

q.q: A legislature authorizes $200 million of spending while the central bank adjusts its monetary stance. Which accountability distinction is valid?
options: The Treasury must approve every private bank loan because it authorizes public spending
Fiscal authorities authorize spending; the central bank implements monetary policy under its legal mandate and accountability framework
The central bank writes the spending appropriation whenever monetary policy is independent
Independence means the central bank has no legal mandate or reporting obligation
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The Treasury must approve every private bank loan because it authorizes public spending” in this central bank and federal reserve task.
q.feedback: Institutional separation distinguishes fiscal appropriations from monetary policy. Operational independence is compatible with a legislated mandate and accountability, not an absence of constraints.

q.q: A restaurant market has many sellers, but each offers a differentiated experience. Which statement is best?
options: The market may be competitive in a broad sense without meeting the strict price-taking benchmark.
The large number of restaurants makes each a price taker despite customers’ preferences for particular experiences.
Differentiation gives each restaurant the pricing freedom of a sole supplier because other dining experiences are distinct.
Competition should be assessed only through price differences, since differences in service quality do not affect buyer choice.
q.commonError: Treating market structures as all-or-nothing labels.
q.feedback: Many restaurants can compete for customers even when differentiated experiences give individual sellers some price discretion. Differentiation means the strict identical-product price-taking benchmark need not hold, but competing restaurants can still constrain each other’s prices.

q.q: A firm in a competitive market raises price above the market price while rivals do not. The likely result is:
options: Higher sales because price signals quality.
A sharp loss of customers to close substitutes.
No change because buyers cannot switch.
Automatic market-wide inflation.
q.commonError: Assuming a small firm can raise price without losing demand.
q.feedback: Buyers can switch to other sellers offering the same or similar product.

q.q: A licensing rule sharply limits new sellers. What is the most direct competitive effect?
options: The rule guarantees lower prices.
The rule creates perfect information.
Reduced entry can increase the market power of existing sellers.
The rule makes every firm a price taker.
q.commonError: Ignoring how entry barriers protect incumbents.
q.feedback: Barriers can weaken competitive pressure and preserve market power.

q.q: A market has many sellers, but buyers face high search costs and cannot compare prices. Why might price-taking be weakened?
options: Many sellers always eliminate market power.
High search costs strengthen competition by making buyers compare prices more carefully.
Price comparison is unrelated to competition.
Information frictions can give individual sellers some pricing discretion.
q.commonError: Assuming seller count alone determines competitiveness.
q.feedback: Competition also depends on buyer information and ability to switch.

q.q: A market appears to have many separate sellers, but four firms own most capacity through subsidiaries. What should an analyst examine?
options: Only the number of storefronts.
Whether prices are written in dollars.
Whether consumers enjoy variety.
Which firms control capacity, rather than the number of brands.
q.commonError: Counting labels instead of economic control.
q.feedback: Competitive pressure depends on independent control of capacity and decisions.

q.q: A market has free entry but strong network effects favor the largest platform. What is the best conclusion?
options: Legal freedom to enter makes the incumbent face perfectly elastic demand despite its user network.
Formal entry may be easy while effective competition remains weak.
Network effects remove the incumbent’s advantage because every entrant can start with an equally valuable user network.
The incumbent’s user advantage implies formal entry is restricted, so the premise of free entry cannot hold.
q.commonError: Equating legal permission to enter with practical competitive viability.
q.feedback: Permission to enter does not ensure that a new platform can attract enough users to compete effectively. When a platform becomes more valuable as its user base grows, the incumbent’s network can be an entry obstacle even without legal restrictions. That advantage does not establish perfectly elastic demand or equal starting networks.

q.q: A price taker is a seller that:
options: Accepts the market price because its own output is too small to move it.
Sets the market price for all firms.
Has no production costs.
Faces no buyers.
q.commonError: confuses_price_taker_with_price_maker
q.feedback: Price takers choose output but cannot materially influence the market price.

q.commonError: Treating all price increases as inflation even when quality or product variety improves.
q.q: Which scenario combines two CPI biases at once?
options: A new streaming service draws consumers from expensive cable
A worker becomes unemployed during a recession
Exports rise faster than imports
Government purchases increase
q.feedback: New goods and substitution both complicate CPI measurement.

q.q: Prices of domestically produced aircraft exports rise while imported smartphones bought by households become cheaper. Which combination is plausible?
options: The GDP deflator rises while the CPI falls
The CPI rises while the GDP deflator falls
Both indexes must rise because one price increased
Both indexes must fall because consumers buy smartphones
q.commonError: Ignores whether a priced item is imported, exported, consumed, or part of domestic investment.
q.feedback: The aircraft exports are domestic production and enter the GDP deflator, so their higher prices push it up. Imported smartphones enter the CPI but not the GDP deflator; their lower price can pull CPI inflation down.

q.q: Crowding out reduces new machinery purchases, while depreciation and all other growth determinants are unchanged. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: The existing capital stock falls immediately by the full amount of forgone investment
Future output must decline by exactly the reduction in machinery spending
The capital stock is unchanged because investment affects only financial claims
The future capital stock is lower than otherwise, but may still grow
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The existing capital stock falls immediately by the full amount of forgone investment” in this crowding out and capital formation task.
q.feedback: Less gross investment means less addition to the capital stock than in the counterfactual. The stock can still grow if remaining investment exceeds depreciation, so an absolute decline is not implied.

q.q: A government raises purchases with net taxes unchanged. Private-saving behavior is unchanged. Which sequence describes the fiscal consequence?
options: Private saving falls but public saving is unchanged, because government purchases are household consumption
Public saving rises and the budget moves toward surplus, reducing the need to issue government debt
Public saving falls and the budget moves toward deficit, increasing borrowing needs if the shortfall is debt-financed
Public saving falls but issuing debt counts as revenue, so borrowing restores the budget balance
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Private saving falls but public saving is unchanged, because government purchases are household consumption” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
q.feedback: With net taxes unchanged, higher government purchases reduce public saving T − G and move the budget toward deficit. Borrowing can finance the shortfall, but debt issuance does not count as revenue or reverse the decline in public saving.

q.q: The deficit becomes smaller, nominal debt rises, and debt-to-GDP falls. Which combination can explain all three facts?
options: A surplus raises debt
Debt falls faster than GDP while the annual deficit becomes larger
Debt rises, but nominal GDP grows faster
A balanced budget erases existing debt while nominal GDP remains unchanged
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Debt falls faster than GDP while the annual deficit becomes larger” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
q.feedback: The deficit can still add to nominal debt, while faster GDP growth lowers the debt ratio.

q.q: The overall deficit is $40, including interest outlays of $80. Define the primary balance as revenues minus noninterest outlays. Which diagnosis follows?
options: The primary balance is a $40 surplus even though the overall budget is in deficit
The primary balance is a $120 deficit because interest is added a second time
The primary balance is zero because all deficits consist entirely of interest
The primary balance equals the outstanding debt stock of $40
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The primary balance is a $120 deficit because interest is added a second time” in this deficits debt and government borrowing task.
q.feedback: Overall deficit = primary deficit + interest. Primary deficit = 40−80=−40, so there is a primary surplus of 40. Flow definitions matter.

q.q: The price of peanut butter rises. If jelly is a complement, what happens in the jelly market?
options: Demand for jelly decreases
Demand for jelly increases
Supply of jelly decreases
Quantity demanded of jelly increases
q.commonError: gets_complement_effect_backwards
q.feedback: Peanut butter and jelly are complements. If peanut butter gets more expensive, demand for jelly falls.

q.q: The price of bus rides rises. If subway rides are substitutes, what happens in the subway market?
options: Demand for subway rides increases
Demand for subway rides decreases
Supply of subway rides decreases
Quantity supplied of bus rides increases
q.commonError: gets_substitute_effect_backwards
q.feedback: When the price of a substitute rises, demand for the other good increases.

q.q: Consumers expect the price of coffee to fall next month. What happens to current demand for coffee, other things equal?
options: Current demand decreases
Current demand increases
Current quantity supplied increases
Supply shifts left
q.commonError: gets_future_price_expectation_effect_backwards
q.feedback: If buyers expect a lower future price, they delay purchases, reducing current demand.

q.q: A product gets cheaper because supply increases. Students say demand increased because quantity sold rose. What is the error?
options: They confused an increase in quantity demanded with an increase in demand
They correctly identified a demand shift
They confused a price floor with a price ceiling
They ignored that supply can never change price
q.commonError: calls_quantity_demanded_change_demand_increase
q.feedback: If price falls because supply increases, buyers move along the demand curve. Quantity demanded rises, but demand itself does not shift.

q.q: The price of a substitute for coffee rises. What happens in the coffee market, holding other factors constant?
options: Demand for coffee increases, raising equilibrium price and quantity
Quantity demanded of coffee decreases along the same curve
Supply of coffee increases because coffee is now profitable
Demand for coffee decreases because substitutes are now expensive
q.commonError: confuses_substitutes_with_complements
q.feedback: When a substitute becomes more expensive, demand for the original good rises.

q.q: The price of peanut butter falls. What happens to the demand for jelly, assuming they are complements?
options: Demand for jelly increases
Quantity demanded of jelly falls along the same curve
Supply of jelly decreases
Demand for jelly decreases because peanut butter is cheaper
q.commonError: moves_along_jelly_demand_when_related_good_price_changes
q.feedback: A lower price for a complement increases demand for the related good.

q.q: An economy faces higher oil prices and falling output. Why is aggressive AD stimulus risky?
options: It may restore output but add inflation pressure
It must lower prices and raise unemployment
It shifts SRAS right without cost
It removes the natural rate
q.commonError: Thinking supply-shock policy has no tradeoff.
q.feedback: Stimulating AD can support output but may worsen inflation after an adverse supply shock.

q.q: A supply shock raises prices and lowers output. The central bank tightens policy to fight inflation. What is the likely short-run danger?
options: Output falls further below potential
Inflation rises because AD expands
Unemployment falls below natural
SRAS shifts right immediately
q.commonError: Ignoring output costs of tightening after a supply shock.
q.feedback: Tightening reduces AD and may lower inflation pressure, but it can worsen the output decline.

q.q: An economy experiences an adverse supply shock. Policymakers fully stabilize real output with expansionary demand policy. What tradeoff follows?
options: The price level returns to its original value once output is restored.
Inflation and unemployment both fall because the policy removes the supply shock.
Output is stabilized, but inflation pressure becomes stronger.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because aggregate demand rises.
q.commonError: Assuming demand policy can reverse a supply shock without an inflation cost.
q.feedback: Expansionary demand policy can offset the output loss from an adverse supply shock, but it intensifies inflation pressure.

q.q: Real output rises while the price level falls. Which pair of simultaneous shifts can produce that pattern?
options: Both curves shift left, with the demand shift dominating the output effect.
Demand shifts right while supply shifts left, with demand dominating output.
Demand shifts left while supply shifts right, with demand dominating output.
Both curves shift right, with the supply shift dominating the price effect.
q.commonError: Matching one observed outcome to one curve while ignoring the second observed outcome.
q.feedback: Higher output can come from either shift, but a falling price level requires the rightward supply shift to dominate the demand effect.

q.q: Aggregate demand rises while short-run aggregate supply falls. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Real output rises, while the price level is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output rises.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
Both the price level and real output fall.
q.commonError: Claiming certainty about output when the two shocks move output in opposite directions.
q.feedback: Both shifts raise the price level, but aggregate demand raises output while adverse supply lowers it.

q.q: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply rises. Which outcome is certain?
options: Real output falls, while the price level is uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output is uncertain.
q.commonError: Missing the shared price-level direction of the two shifts.
q.feedback: A demand contraction and favorable supply shock both lower the price level, but they push output in opposite directions.

q.q: After an adverse supply shock, policymakers use expansionary demand policy to restore output. Which risk remains?
options: The price level may rise even more than it did from the original shock.
Unemployment must rise because aggregate demand increased.
Short-run aggregate supply automatically returns to its old position.
The economy must move below potential output.
q.commonError: Assuming output stabilization eliminates the inflation tradeoff.
q.feedback: Demand expansion can support output after a supply shock, but it adds inflation pressure rather than repairing supply.

q.q: If banks lend more aggressively from excess reserves, the money supply rises mainly because
options: new loans create new deposits as funds are spent and redeposited
the Fed prints commodity money for each loan
M1 excludes bank deposits
borrowers destroy checking accounts when they borrow
q.commonError: thinking bank lending only transfers existing money without deposit creation
q.feedback: Bank lending creates deposits as loan proceeds are spent and redeposited through the banking system.

q.q: If the simple money multiplier falls from 10 to 4, what happened to the reserve ratio?
options: It rose from 10 percent to 25 percent.
It fell from 25 percent to 10 percent.
It rose from 4 percent to 10 percent.
It fell from 10 percent to 4 percent.
q.commonError: thinking a smaller multiplier means a smaller reserve ratio
q.feedback: The reserve ratio is 1/multiplier. A multiplier of 10 means 10 percent; a multiplier of 4 means 25 percent.

q.q: A disinflation announcement is not credible, and wage contracts embed 6% inflation. What makes immediate costless adjustment unlikely?
options: Aggregate demand cannot affect inflation
Deflation is required before unemployment changes
Expected inflation and nominal contracts may adjust slowly
The LRPC must shift left before policy begins
q.commonError: Assumes credibility mechanically eliminates every short-run output cost.
q.feedback: Credibility can speed expectations adjustment, but disinflation costs depend on model assumptions and wage-price adjustment.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: Which policy mix is most likely to support sustained productivity growth rather than only a temporary boost?
options: Education, investment, property rights, trade, and research support
One-time stimulus checks only
Price ceilings on all capital goods
Discouraging foreign investment and innovation
q.feedback: Sustained growth comes from policies that improve capital, skills, innovation, and institutions.

q.commonError: Focusing on short-run spending instead of policies that raise long-run productivity.
q.q: A country funds education but blocks firms from adopting new technologies and discourages investment. What is the likely issue?
options: Skills need complementary capital and technology
Education alone guarantees growth
Technology restrictions raise productivity
Investment is unrelated to output per worker
q.feedback: Productivity growth usually requires complementary gains in skills, capital, and technology.

q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Research incentives instantly eliminate every current demand shortfall without a timing lag” in this economic growth policy task.
q.q: A country has idle capacity after a recession and weak long-run research incentives. Which policy pairing addresses the two different problems?
options: Research incentives instantly eliminate every current demand shortfall without a timing lag
Both problems require only more nominal money because all real output is money-determined
Demand stabilization can use idle capacity; stronger research incentives can improve future productive capacity
Demand stabilization permanently raises technology by the same amount as spending, making research incentives unnecessary
q.feedback: Closing a demand gap and shifting the long-run productive frontier are different objectives. Research has a capacity channel and timing; a temporary demand boost is not a substitute for it.

q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Mandate a higher nominal GDP target and infer that skills must improve” in this economic growth policy task.
q.q: Firms underinvest in training because employees may leave with their new skills. Which proposal targets that mechanism while recognizing a resource tradeoff?
options: Subsidize current consumption; treat the resulting spending as equivalent to transferable training.
Co-finance transferable training; compare spillover benefits with the funds' alternative uses.
Protect current jobs from new technology; treat lower mobility as increased skill formation.
Raise the nominal GDP target; treat its dollar increase as additional human capital.
q.feedback: Training can create spillovers that private firms do not fully capture. Co-financing may address that incentive, but training uses resources and its social return must justify the cost.

q.q: A policy model predicts large benefits, but the data come from a different population and period. What is the central concern?
options: Whether the evidence generalizes to the current setting.
Whether the policy has a money price.
Whether economists may use models.
Whether positive analysis is always normative.
q.commonError: Assuming evidence transfers automatically across settings.
q.feedback: Policy advice must consider whether evidence is applicable to the target population and context.

q.q: An economist is employed by an agency that benefits from a favorable estimate. What practice best protects credibility?
options: Publish the chosen model with full calculations, omitting the agency relationship to keep the report technical.
Disclose the agency interest, assumptions, alternatives and uncertainty so others can assess the estimate.
Have an agency colleague check the arithmetic, then report one point estimate to avoid confusing readers.
Report an interval from the chosen model, leaving model selection and other reasonable versions of the model to the agency.
q.commonError: Ignoring incentives facing analysts.
q.feedback: Disclosure must address both the institutional interest and methodological discretion. Arithmetic review or an uncertainty interval alone does not reveal how model selection could favor the agency.

q.q: A policy has a positive expected net benefit but a small chance of catastrophic loss. Which addition is necessary?
options: A claim that averages eliminate risk.
Removal of all low-probability outcomes.
Risk analysis beyond the expected-value calculation.
A conclusion based only on sunk costs.
q.commonError: Treating expected value as a complete policy criterion.
q.feedback: Low-probability, high-cost outcomes may matter even when expected net benefits are positive.

q.q: A pilot worked elsewhere but institutions differ locally. What is the key warning?
options: A successful pilot automatically generalizes to other settings
Institutional differences matter only for normative judgments
A large effect elsewhere guarantees a large local effect.
Evidence may not transfer to the new setting
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: An efficient proposal conflicts with a legal-rights goal. What follows?
options: The efficient proposal must be adopted
Efficiency evidence does not uniquely decide social desirability
The legal-rights goal is irrelevant to policy evaluation
The conflict proves the proposal is economically inefficient.
q.commonError: Treating efficiency as the only criterion of social desirability.
q.feedback: Economic analysis clarifies tradeoffs but does not uniquely rank every social goal.

q.q: A recommendation changes under plausible assumptions. What should the economist do?
options: Report only the baseline estimate
Use the assumption that produces the most favorable result
Report sensitivity rather than one certain answer
Delay all advice until uncertainty is eliminated.
q.commonError: Presenting an estimate as a guarantee.
q.feedback: Responsible advice reports assumptions, uncertainty, and plausible unintended consequences.

q.q: An economist recommends a policy because it maximizes total surplus, while citizens prioritize equal treatment. The disagreement is primarily about:
options: The arithmetic definition of surplus.
The normative criterion used to rank outcomes.
Whether incentives exist.
The distinction between micro and macro topics.
q.commonError: Calling a value disagreement an empirical error.
q.feedback: Economic analysis can measure consequences, but ranking competing values requires a normative criterion.

q.q: Fiscal expansion raises AD through the multiplier, but interest rates rise and investment falls. Which description best fits the final result?
options: Initial AD shift partly offset by crowding out
SRAS shift fully offset by lower taxes
LRPC shift partly offset by higher inflation
Money demand shift fully offset by M1
q.commonError: Treating the multiplier as the final effect every time.
q.feedback: Fiscal expansion can be amplified by the multiplier but weakened by crowding out.

q.q: If government spending rises, MPC is high, and interest rates do not rise, which effect dominates?
options: Multiplier effect
Crowding out
Monetary neutrality
Adverse supply shock
q.commonError: Assuming crowding out always dominates fiscal policy.
q.feedback: A high MPC strengthens the multiplier, and little interest-rate increase means crowding out is weak.

q.q: If government spending rises, MPC is low, and interest rates rise sharply, which concern dominates?
options: Weak multiplier with strong crowding out
Strong multiplier with no crowding out
Money neutrality with no AD change
Expected inflation with SRPC falling
q.commonError: Ignoring both MPC size and interest-rate effects.
q.feedback: A low MPC weakens the multiplier, while higher rates crowd out private investment.

q.q: If government spending initially shifts AD right by $40 billion and MPC is 0.75, what is the total shift before crowding out?
options: $160 billion
$70 billion
$40 billion
$30 billion
q.commonError: using MPC as the multiplier instead of 1 divided by 1 minus MPC
q.feedback: With MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is 4. A $40 billion initial shift becomes $160 billion before crowding out.

q.q: A student says fiscal expansion raises AD and therefore can never crowd out investment. What is the best correction?
options: Fiscal expansion can raise AD while higher rates reduce private investment.
Fiscal expansion lowers rates because government borrowing reduces money demand.
Fiscal expansion shifts SRAS right because firms face lower costs.
Fiscal expansion eliminates the multiplier because taxes disappear.
q.commonError: Thinking multiplier effects rule out crowding out.
q.feedback: Fiscal expansion can increase AD, but rising interest rates can reduce investment and offset part of the effect.

q.q: Government spending rises by $70 billion and MPC = 0.8. What is the correct order of AD shifts before crowding out?
options: AD first shifts right by $70 billion, then shifts farther right to a total of $350 billion.
AD first shifts right by $350 billion, then shifts back to $70 billion.
AD shifts left by $70 billion, then left by $350 billion.
AD does not shift because the multiplier only affects money demand.
q.commonError: confusing the initial AD shift with the final multiplier shift
q.feedback: The first AD shift is the direct $70 billion increase in G. With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5, so the final AD shift is $350 billion.

q.q: If MPC = 0.9 and government spending increases by $25 billion, what is the simple multiplier effect on AD before crowding out?
options: $250 billion
$22.5 billion
$27.8 billion
$225 billion
q.commonError: using 0.9 as the multiplier instead of 10
q.feedback: With MPC = 0.9, the multiplier is 10. AD increases by 10 x $25 billion = $250 billion.

q.q: A government raises taxes and increases purchases by the same dollar amount. Which statement is most precise about the immediate AD effects?
options: The two actions must cancel exactly before behavior is considered.
Both actions shift AD right by the same amount.
Taxes enter AD directly as a negative component.
Purchases enter AD directly, while higher taxes reduce consumption indirectly.
q.commonError: Treating taxes as a direct component of aggregate demand.
q.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD; taxes work through disposable income and consumption.

q.q: The government cuts purchases during a recession but also cuts taxes. Which conclusion is valid without knowing the magnitudes and household response?
options: Aggregate demand must rise.
The two policies always cancel exactly.
The net direction of aggregate demand is ambiguous.
Aggregate demand must fall.
q.commonError: Assuming one policy label determines the combined outcome.
q.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left, while a tax cut tends to shift it right; magnitudes matter.

q.q: A real depreciation occurs in the currency market. How does that change connect to aggregate demand?
options: The depreciation shifts short-run aggregate supply left
Higher net exports shift aggregate demand right
Lower net exports shift aggregate demand left
Domestic investment becomes zero
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The depreciation shifts short-run aggregate supply left” in this foreign exchange market task.
q.feedback: Real depreciation makes domestic goods relatively cheaper, tending to raise NX; because NX is an AD component, aggregate demand increases.

q.q: Specialization raises combined output, but a proposed exchange rate lies above both producers’ costs for the exported good. What follows?
options: Higher output creates potential gains, but this rate will not benefit both sides
Every feasible exchange must share the production gain.
The higher-cost producer now has comparative advantage
Both sides are strictly better off because specialization occurred
q.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
q.feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

q.q: As producers specialize further, their opportunity costs rise. What does this imply about how much specialization is needed to gain from trade?
options: Both producers can gain through specialization without either specializing completely
Both producers must always specialize completely.
Opportunity cost becomes irrelevant after exchange
Absolute advantage fixes every output
q.commonError: Skipping a required link among opportunity cost, specialization, exchange, and the autarky comparison.
q.feedback: With increasing opportunity cost, producing more of a good requires giving up progressively more of the other good. Reallocation can create gains while relative marginal costs differ, but the rising cost can make further specialization unattractive before either producer specializes completely. Absolute productivity alone does not determine that stopping point.

q.q: Combined consumption rises by 9 units, but one party gains 11 while the other loses 2. What is the correct evaluation?
options: Aggregate gain exists, but the trade is not mutually beneficial
Both parties gain because their combined consumption increases.
The losing party has advantage in both goods
Each gain must be reset to 4.5
q.commonError: Equating positive aggregate gains with equal or universal individual gains.
q.feedback: Total gains and their distribution are distinct; terms of trade allocate the modeled surplus.

q.q: Suppose learning-by-doing lowers a nation’s future opportunity cost in a good it does not currently produce. What does this imply?
options: Current comparative advantage may not fully describe future comparative advantage.
Opportunity costs can never change over time.
The nation must already have absolute advantage in that good.
Trade eliminates any reason to consider future productivity.
q.commonError: Assuming the static model settles every long-run policy question.
q.feedback: Investment and learning can alter future relative costs, so dynamic considerations may matter.

q.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
q.q: A government sends $1,000 unemployment checks to households, and households spend the full amount on groceries. What is the GDP effect?
options: The transfer is excluded; grocery purchases count as consumption
Both the transfer and groceries count, so GDP rises by $2,000
Neither counts because government is involved
Only the transfer counts as government purchases
q.feedback: Transfer payments are not purchases of current goods and services, but later household spending can count as consumption.

q.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
q.q: A U.S. household buys a $40,000 car produced in Germany. In U.S. GDP accounting, what happens?
options: Consumption rises $40,000 and net exports fall $40,000; GDP is unchanged
Consumption rises and GDP rises by $40,000
Investment rises and imports are ignored
Government purchases rise and GDP is unchanged
q.feedback: Imported consumer goods enter consumption but are subtracted through imports in net exports, so domestic GDP does not rise.

q.commonError: Adding imports instead of subtracting them through net exports.
q.q: If C = $15T, I = $4T, G = $6T, imports = $5T, and GDP = $23T, what are exports?

q.commonError: Mixing up the GDP expenditure components or forgetting the C + I + G + NX identity.
q.q: A household buys a newly built condo for $250,000 and pays $3,000 in property taxes. Which is the best GDP treatment?
options: The condo is investment; the property tax is not current output
Both count as consumption
The condo is consumption and the tax is government purchases
Neither counts
q.feedback: New residential construction is investment. A tax payment is not itself government purchase of a final good or service.

q.q: The same dollar penalty sharply changes behavior for low-income households but barely affects high-income households. What does this show?
options: All people respond identically to a given dollar amount.
The penalty is not an incentive.
Responses depend on constraints and the size of the incentive relative to resources.
Income has no role in marginal choices.
q.commonError: Assuming uniform responses across people.
q.feedback: A fixed incentive can have different marginal importance for different decision-makers.

q.q: A hospital is paid for each procedure but penalized for readmissions. Which response best reflects both incentives?
options: It may increase profitable procedures while investing in follow-up that lowers readmissions
It must reduce every procedure because penalties dominate rewards
It will ignore follow-up entirely because only direct procedure payments can ever affect hospital behavior
The payment design guarantees the socially optimal treatment mix
q.commonError: Reasoning from only one component of a multi-part payment system.
q.feedback: Procedure payments and readmission penalties act on different behavioral margins.

q.q: A deductible rises from $100 to $1,000. Which prediction is best without knowing patient income, health risk, or alternatives?
options: Use of covered services tends to fall, but response size can vary widely
Every patient reduces covered care by exactly the same percentage after the deductible change
No response is possible because insurance already exists
The higher deductible guarantees better health decisions
q.commonError: Inferring an identical or guaranteed response from a common price change.
q.feedback: The higher out-of-pocket cost creates directional pressure, while circumstances shape magnitude.

q.q: A police department rewards citation counts. Citations rise, public trust falls, and serious-case work receives less time. Which conclusion is warranted?
options: The metric changed behavior but did not capture the department’s full objective
Falling trust proves the citation reward cannot influence officer behavior or case priorities in any meaningful way
More citations establish that public safety necessarily improved
Economic analysis requires moral approval of the reward
q.commonError: Treating a rewarded count as identical to the underlying public objective.
q.feedback: The reward affects behavior, but the observed metric omits trust and case importance.

q.q: Why can a small probability of a severe penalty sometimes have little deterrent effect?
options: People may discount unlikely enforcement or misperceive the risk.
Only rewards influence behavior.
The expected cost is always equal to the maximum penalty.
Penalties have no opportunity cost.
q.commonError: Ignoring enforcement probability and perceptions.
q.feedback: Behavior depends on the expected and perceived consequence, not just the statutory maximum.

q.q: A congestion charge is announced, but drivers believe cameras identify only 5% of violators. Which factor most limits deterrence?
options: The low perceived probability of paying the charge
The charge is negative rather than positive
Driving has benefits as well as costs
A legal charge cannot change expected costs
q.commonError: Ignoring perceived enforcement when evaluating an incentive’s strength.
q.feedback: The expected cost depends on both the charge and the chance it is imposed.

q.q: A housing program withdraws $1 of aid for each $1 of additional earnings over a threshold. Which behavioral pressure follows?
options: Earning just above the threshold may provide little immediate net gain
Every recipient stops working completely
The rule rewards every additional dollar of earnings with an equal dollar of net income
Aid withdrawal is an outcome rather than an incentive
q.commonError: Ignoring how benefit withdrawal changes the payoff to extra earnings.
q.feedback: The phaseout can sharply reduce the net benefit of crossing the earnings threshold.

q.q: A transit agency offers off-peak discounts. Flexible riders shift trips, while shift workers cannot. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: The price incentive changes trip timing mainly for riders with feasible alternatives
The discount is not an incentive because some riders cannot respond
All riders receive identical benefits from changing travel time
The policy guarantees total ridership will rise
q.commonError: Treating inability to respond as evidence that no incentive exists.
q.feedback: The discount changes relative prices, but schedule constraints determine who can act on it.

q.q: A delivery platform guarantees a minimum hourly payment only while drivers are actively carrying orders. Which response is plausible?
options: Drivers may favor longer trips or avoid unpaid waiting when choosing orders
Every driver accepts the shortest available trip
The guarantee removes all opportunity costs of time
Payment rules cannot change which orders drivers select
q.commonError: Ignoring how compensation changes the opportunity cost of time and order selection.
q.feedback: The rule changes which activities count as paid time, altering the relative payoff to orders.

q.q: A city raises water prices after a monthly allowance and also publishes neighborhood conservation rankings. What response should be expected?
options: Price and status pressures may reduce use by different amounts across households
The ranking is irrelevant because only prices are incentives
Every household cuts water use by the same quantity
Lower use is guaranteed wherever both incentives exist
q.commonError: Assuming one incentive type matters or that responses are uniform.
q.feedback: Both monetary cost and social comparison can affect use, with varied strength.

q.q: An energy plan combines a peak-hour surcharge, a monthly conservation badge, and a rebate for smart thermostats. Which analysis is strongest?
options: The surcharge targets peak timing, the badge targets status, and the rebate changes equipment cost; responses depend on constraints.
The surcharge and badge both reward lower total use, while the rebate leaves the cost of conservation equipment unchanged.
The rebate targets peak timing, the surcharge targets equipment purchase, and the badge reveals each household’s willingness to pay.
The three measures all lower the same marginal electricity price, so peak-use changes identify their separate contributions.
q.commonError: Collapsing several incentives and response margins into one guaranteed outcome.
q.feedback: These incentives operate on different margins: timing, social recognition and equipment adoption. Neither a uniform response nor lower total consumption follows from a peak-use decline.

q.q: A university receives funding for degrees completed on time. Advising improves, but difficult required courses are weakened. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: Funding rewards completion speed, so advising effort and lower course standards can both improve the metric without equal learning gains.
Funding rewards educational quality, so faster completion and easier courses jointly establish more learning per enrolled student.
Easier courses explain completion gains entirely, so advising improvements cannot contribute to the measured funding outcome.
Faster completion reduces students’ time costs, so course standards have no additional role in evaluating the policy’s net benefit.
q.commonError: Equating the observable target with the complete educational objective.
q.feedback: A completion metric can reward both useful advising and weakened standards. Evaluating educational success requires learning evidence in addition to completion and time savings.

q.q: A health insurer waives copays for preventive visits but raises emergency-room copays. Which response is most defensible?
options: Lower preventive prices and higher emergency prices encourage substitution, but access and urgent needs constrain which patients can switch.
The price changes chiefly reduce total visits; patients with limited preventive access can substitute as readily as other patients.
The preventive subsidy raises income rather than relative prices; changes in emergency use therefore identify only the copay increase.
Emergency use should fall most for unavoidable acute cases; elective preventive care is least responsive to the lower copay.
q.commonError: Predicting certain, uniform substitution from a common payment schedule.
q.feedback: Relative prices favor prevention, but substitution requires access and medical feasibility. Acute emergencies and barriers to preventive care limit the response.

q.q: A platform threatens suspension for false listings, but enforcement reviews only complaints from paying users. What response is most plausible?
options: Expected sanctions differ by customer group, so sellers may redirect deception toward users whose complaints do not trigger review.
A uniform suspension penalty creates equal deterrence across users, so different complaint review rules mainly affect paperwork.
Paying users receive more review, so sellers face a stronger incentive to deceive them in order to cover expected sanctions.
The threat discourages entry by dishonest sellers, so surviving sellers’ choices between user groups are unaffected by enforcement.
q.commonError: Ignoring how selective enforcement redirects behavior.
q.feedback: Expected sanctions combine the penalty with the probability of review. Restricting review to paying-user complaints changes the relative payoff to targeting other users.

q.q: A government contract pays builders for finishing early and penalizes visible defects, but not hidden maintenance problems. What risk remains?
options: Rewards cover speed and observable defects, so effort can shift from hidden durability toward the measured dimensions.
The defect penalty prices all quality losses, so earlier completion also establishes greater hidden durability.
The speed reward and defect penalty create opposing incentives, so their combined effect on effort must be zero.
Maintenance is paid later, so hidden durability is a sunk cost and should be excluded from evaluating the contract.
q.commonError: Assuming measured dimensions represent total performance.
q.feedback: When hidden maintenance problems are not penalized, the contract can reward speed and visible quality while encouraging substitution away from durability. Later costs are not thereby sunk.

q.q: A criminal fine is tripled while the probability of detection falls by two-thirds. Without more information, what can be concluded?
options: Expected monetary penalties are unchanged, while perceived detection and risk attitudes can still alter deterrence.
Expected monetary penalties triple, while lower detection only changes the timing of the payment.
Expected monetary penalties fall by two-thirds, while the larger fine affects only the maximum possible loss.
Expected monetary penalties are unchanged, so deterrence must remain unchanged for every risk attitude.
q.commonError: Using only penalty size or only detection probability.
q.feedback: If detection falls to one-third and the fine triples, probability times fine is unchanged. Equal expected money costs do not establish equal perceived or risk-adjusted deterrence.

q.q: A conservation policy combines a usage fee, public recognition, and exemptions for medical needs. Which assessment is most defensible?
options: Different households face different effective incentives, so response and burden will vary
The usage fee guarantees identical reductions for all households
Recognition is irrelevant because it is not money
Exemptions prove the policy has no behavioral effect
q.commonError: Ignoring multiple incentive types, constraints, and exemptions.
q.feedback: Prices, status, and exemptions change payoffs differently across households.

q.q: A retiree benefit is indexed to overall CPI, but retirees buy a systematically different basket. What limitation remains?
options: The benefit should be deflated with the GDP deflator only
CPI cannot measure any consumer prices
The chosen index may not match the retiree’s actual cost changes
Indexation guarantees identical costs for every household
q.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
q.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

q.q: A salary adjustment uses last year’s CPI while inflation accelerates this year. What can happen before the next adjustment?
options: Current inflation becomes irrelevant
Purchasing power can temporarily fall
Real value must rise because the contract is indexed
The nominal salary must decline
q.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
q.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

q.q: A pension is fully CPI-indexed, but quality gains make CPI overstate true living-cost growth. What is the likely real effect?
options: The pension must lose nominal value throughout the entire inflation-adjustment period
Indexation eliminates quality measurement issues
The GDP deflator must rise by the same amount
The pension can gain purchasing power relative to the true cost of living
q.commonError: Assumes an indexed contract guarantees an exact real outcome in every circumstance.
q.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

q.q: If all prices rise but incomes rise by the same percentage, why can inflation still be costly?
options: It causes shoe-leather and menu costs, tax distortions, distorted relative-price signals, and redistribution.
It has no costs if incomes rise at all.
It only affects people who never buy goods.
It permanently raises real wages.
q.commonError: thinking inflation is harmless whenever nominal incomes rise
q.feedback: Inflation can still impose real costs through behavior changes, price adjustment costs, distortions, and redistribution.

q.q: A student says inflation makes everyone poorer because all prices rise. What is the best response?
options: Incomes can rise too; inflation still causes costs and redistribution.
Inflation never has costs if any wage rises.
Inflation only affects creditors and no one else.
Inflation lowers all nominal incomes by definition.
q.commonError: thinking inflation's only effect is higher prices with no nominal income adjustment
q.feedback: Rising prices alone do not establish that everyone loses purchasing power: nominal incomes and fixed contracts matter. Inflation can still use resources, distort decisions and redistribute wealth.

q.q: A country uses seigniorage heavily during a fiscal crisis. Which combination is most likely if confidence erodes?
options: Rapid money growth, rising expected inflation, and higher nominal interest rates
Falling money growth, falling expected inflation, and lower nominal interest rates
No change in inflation because money is neutral in the short run
Lower price levels and higher money value immediately
q.commonError: thinking seigniorage is free revenue with no expectations effect
q.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations, and higher expected inflation pushes nominal interest rates up.

q.q: A government prints money to finance spending, expected inflation rises, and households reduce desired real cash balances. Which concern is most complete?
options: Households holding less money automatically raises real output enough to offset the inflation-tax burden and preserve seigniorage revenue.
Inflation-tax finance can erode real balances and become harder to sustain as people avoid holding money.
Lower money demand guarantees a stable price level despite continued money creation.
Printing money eliminates the need to consider inflation because seigniorage is a real resource.
q.commonError: Treats money creation as a costless financing source regardless of public money demand.
q.feedback: Heavy money finance can raise inflation expectations and reduce desired real money balances, making continued reliance on seigniorage increasingly disruptive.

q.q: Which statement best connects a negative AD shock across AD-AS and Phillips curve models?
options: AD shifts left; output falls; unemployment rises; inflation falls
SRAS shifts left; output falls; unemployment falls; inflation rises
AD shifts right; output rises; unemployment rises; inflation falls
LRAS shifts right; output falls; unemployment rises; inflation rises
q.commonError: Confusing demand shocks with supply shocks across models.
q.feedback: A negative AD shock lowers output and inflation, which maps to higher unemployment and lower inflation on the SRPC.

q.q: Which statement best connects an adverse supply shock across AD-AS and Phillips curve models?
options: SRAS shifts left; output falls; inflation and unemployment rise
AD shifts left; output falls; inflation and unemployment fall
SRAS shifts right; output rises; inflation and unemployment rise
AD shifts right; output rises; inflation falls and unemployment rises
q.commonError: Missing stagflation across both models.
q.feedback: An adverse supply shock lowers output and raises prices, mapping to higher unemployment and higher inflation.

q.q: A student sees inflation rising and immediately recommends contractionary policy. What missing diagnosis matters most?
options: Whether inflation comes from AD growth or a supply shock
Whether M1 includes checkable deposits
Whether currency is fiat or commodity money
Whether the FOMC has seven governors
q.commonError: Treating all inflation as excess demand.
q.feedback: Inflation from excess AD and inflation from an adverse supply shock create different policy tradeoffs.

q.q: An adverse supply shock hits, and the Fed accommodates it. What happens in the Phillips curve model?
options: SRPC shifts up and policy may move along the new curve
SRPC shifts down and policy moves to lower inflation
LRPC shifts left and unemployment falls forever
SRPC stays fixed and unemployment must fall
q.commonError: Ignoring both the shock shift and policy movement.
q.feedback: The supply shock shifts SRPC up; accommodation may reduce unemployment pressure but adds inflation pressure along the new curve.

q.q: The economy has high inflation but unemployment is also above natural. Which policy problem is most likely?
options: Supply-side inflation, not simple excess demand
Pure demand boom with no supply issue
Money neutrality in the short run
A permanent Phillips curve improvement
q.commonError: Treating high inflation as always caused by excess AD.
q.feedback: High inflation with above-natural unemployment points toward an adverse supply shock or worsened expectations, not a clean demand boom.

q.q: The economy starts at natural output. A demand boom pushes output above potential and inflation rises. Which policy assessment is strongest?
options: Demand expansion can close the gap sooner; without it, rising wages/expected prices permanently shift LRAS right
Demand tightening can close the gap sooner; without it, rising wages/expected prices can shift SRAS left toward potential
Demand tightening can close the gap sooner; without it, rising wages/expected prices shift SRAS right farther above potential
Demand expansion can close the gap sooner; without it, rising wages/expected prices shift SRAS left toward potential
q.commonError: Treating above-potential output as permanent growth.
q.feedback: A demand boom can push output above potential in the short run, but expected prices and wages adjust, returning output toward natural.

q.q: The economy starts at natural output. Oil prices surge, output falls, and inflation rises. Which policy warning is strongest?
options: Stimulating AD can recover output but risks even higher inflation; tightening can restrain inflation but worsens unemployment.
Stimulating AD lowers inflation and unemployment because supply shocks are solved by more spending.
Tightening AD raises output because firms respond to lower demand by expanding production.
Doing nothing instantly restores output because expected prices adjust before unemployment rises.
q.commonError: Thinking adverse supply shocks have an easy policy fix.
q.feedback: A negative supply shock creates stagflation, so policy faces a real tradeoff between output losses and inflation pressure.

q.q: Output and inflation are falling while unemployment is rising. Which diagnosis and policy pairing is strongest?
options: Negative AD shock; expansionary policy can shift AD back right.
Adverse supply shock; expansionary policy shifts SRAS right.
Positive AD shock; contractionary policy shifts AD farther right.
Favorable supply shock; contractionary policy raises output.
q.commonError: Confusing demand recessions with supply shocks.
q.feedback: Falling output and falling inflation point to weak aggregate demand, which maps to higher unemployment and lower inflation.

q.q: The Fed wants lower inflation. Expected inflation is slow to adjust because the policy lacks credibility. Which assessment is strongest?
options: Disinflation likely carries a higher sacrifice ratio.
Disinflation likely lowers unemployment immediately.
Expected inflation shifts SRPC downward instantly.
The long-run Phillips curve becomes downward sloping.
q.commonError: Ignoring credibility in disinflation costs.
q.feedback: If expected inflation adjusts slowly, reducing inflation requires more output and employment pain.

q.q: The Fed announces disinflation, wage contracts adjust quickly, and expected inflation falls before output drops much. Which assessment is strongest?
options: The sacrifice ratio is likely lower than with slow expectations adjustment.
The sacrifice ratio is likely higher because credibility raises unemployment.
The LRPC shifts right because inflation expectations fall quickly.
The SRPC shifts upward because disinflation reduces actual inflation.
q.commonError: Missing how credibility lowers disinflation costs.
q.feedback: Credibility can lower the cost of disinflation by moving expected inflation down faster.

q.q: A student says a tax cut always creates the full multiplier effect. Which correction is best?
options: The final AD shift depends on MPC, saving, expectations, and crowding out.
The final AD shift ignores MPC because taxes only affect SRAS.
The final AD shift must equal zero because fiscal policy cannot shift AD.
The final AD shift becomes infinite when interest rates rise.
q.commonError: Treating the simple multiplier as the guaranteed final effect.
q.feedback: The simple multiplier can be weakened by saving behavior, expectations, and crowding out.

q.q: Congress expands spending during a recession, but the Fed tightens to fight inflation expectations. Which assessment is strongest?
options: Fiscal stimulus may be offset because higher rates weaken investment and AD.
Fiscal stimulus must fully work because monetary policy cannot affect AD.
Fiscal stimulus shifts SRAS right because higher rates lower production costs.
Fiscal stimulus lowers expected inflation because government spending always reduces prices.
q.commonError: Ignoring fiscal-monetary policy interaction.
q.feedback: Monetary tightening can offset fiscal expansion by raising interest rates and reducing investment.

q.q: The economy is below potential, but inflation expectations are rising. Which policy judgment is strongest?
options: Stimulus may support output but could validate inflation expectations.
Tightening always raises output because expectations matter more than AD.
Stimulus shifts LRAS right and lowers expected inflation automatically.
Doing nothing guarantees lower unemployment and lower inflation immediately.
q.commonError: Ignoring the conflict between output stabilization and expectations.
q.feedback: When output is weak but expectations are rising, policy faces a tradeoff between demand support and inflation credibility.

q.q: The economy has high inflation and unemployment above natural. The Fed expands AD to lower unemployment. What danger follows?
options: Unemployment may improve temporarily, but inflation and expectations can worsen.
Inflation must fall because higher AD lowers production costs.
Unemployment must stay below natural because expectations cannot change.
The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is higher.
q.commonError: Ignoring expectations after accommodation.
q.feedback: AD expansion can reduce unemployment temporarily but may worsen inflation and expected inflation.

q.q: A country doubles money growth, but output growth also rises sharply and velocity falls. Which warning is strongest?
options: Do not infer inflation from money growth alone when V and Y change.
Inflation must double because money growth always maps one-for-one.
Inflation must be zero because output growth always dominates.
