Inflation must equal velocity growth because money is neutral.
q.commonError: Using money growth alone without velocity and output.
q.feedback: The quantity equation requires considering money growth, velocity growth, and real output growth together.

q.q: A government finances deficits by printing money. Inflation rises, nominal rates rise, and real balances lose value. Which memo is strongest?
options: The inflation tax reduces money value and expected inflation raises nominal rates.
The policy raises real output permanently because money growth lowers real wages forever.
The policy lowers nominal rates because inflation makes borrowing cheaper for all lenders.
The policy leaves money value unchanged because fiat money has no intrinsic value.
q.commonError: Treating money creation as painless finance.
q.feedback: Printing money can impose an inflation tax, and higher expected inflation raises nominal rates through the Fisher effect.

q.q: The economy is below potential. Fiscal expansion begins, but interest rates rise and inflation expectations increase. Which policy assessment is strongest?
options: The policy may close part of the gap, but crowding out and expectations weaken the case.
The policy permanently lowers unemployment because the SRPC becomes the LRPC.
The policy shifts SRAS right because higher AD lowers production costs.
The policy has no effect because fiscal policy cannot move AD.
q.commonError: Ignoring crowding out and expectations.
q.feedback: Fiscal expansion can support AD, but crowding out and rising inflation expectations can reduce or complicate the effect.

q.q: The economy is above potential, inflation is rising, and unemployment is low. Which policy assessment is strongest?
options: Tighten demand or allow SRAS adjustment; output above potential is not a stable long-run position.
Expand demand further because low unemployment proves the natural rate has fallen.
Hold policy fixed because high inflation guarantees permanently low unemployment.
Shift money demand right because higher rates raise investment.
q.commonError: Treating short-run low unemployment as permanent.
q.feedback: Above-potential output creates inflation pressure and eventually triggers expectation adjustment.

q.q: The economy is below potential after an adverse supply shock, while inflation remains high. Which policy assessment is strongest?
options: There is no clean fix; AD stimulus helps output but risks inflation, while tightening fights inflation but worsens output.
Expansionary fiscal policy is riskless because any recession means inflation must fall immediately.
Contractionary monetary policy is riskless because lower AD shifts SRAS right automatically.
Doing nothing instantly returns output to potential because supply shocks cannot affect employment.
q.commonError: Thinking supply shocks behave like demand recessions.
q.feedback: Adverse supply shocks create a policy bind: supporting output can worsen inflation, while fighting inflation can worsen unemployment.

q.q: The economy begins at natural output. A major input shortage raises production costs. Why is this not a typical demand-side recession?
options: Output falls, but the price level rises, so the shock is supply-side stagflation.
Output falls and the price level falls, so the shock is weak aggregate demand.
Output rises and inflation rises, so the shock is expansionary demand pressure.
Output rises and inflation falls, so the shock is favorable supply growth.
q.commonError: Treating every recession as weak demand.
q.feedback: A negative supply shock lowers output while raising prices, which creates stagflation.

q.q: A recessionary gap appears after aggregate demand falls. Can waiting restore output?
options: Yes, if wages and expected prices fall enough to shift SRAS right.
Yes, if expected prices rise enough to shift SRAS left.
No, because output gaps cannot close without fiscal expansion.
No, because LRAS must shift left to meet actual output.
q.commonError: Missing long-run self-correction after weak demand.
q.feedback: A recessionary gap can close over time if lower wages and expected prices shift SRAS right.

q.q: An expansionary gap appears after aggregate demand rises. Why can unemployment not remain below the natural rate forever?
options: Rising wages and expected prices shift SRAS left and return output to potential.
Falling wages and expected prices shift SRAS right and increase output further.
The LRPC shifts right because unemployment was temporarily low.
The money multiplier rises and permanently lowers the natural rate.
q.commonError: Treating expansionary gaps as permanent growth.
q.feedback: When output is above potential, wages and expected prices rise, shifting SRAS left and restoring natural output.

q.q: The economy is below potential, but the main cause is an oil shock rather than weak spending. Which mistake should be avoided?
options: Treating the problem as a simple AD shortfall with no inflation tradeoff.
Recognizing that output is weak while prices are under upward pressure.
Seeing that fiscal stimulus may help output but worsen inflation.
Noting that the Phillips curve tradeoff has likely worsened.
q.commonError: Misdiagnosing a supply shock as ordinary weak demand.
q.feedback: An oil shock is not a clean demand recession; policy must account for inflation pressure.

q.q: High inflation is caused by an adverse supply shock rather than demand growth. Which response is most defensible?
options: Contraction may reduce inflation pressure but risks deeper output losses.
Expansion must lower inflation because it raises aggregate demand.
Contraction must raise output because lower AD reduces firm costs.
Expansion shifts SRAS right because government spending increases productivity.
q.commonError: Using demand-inflation logic on supply-shock inflation.
q.feedback: With supply-shock inflation, contraction can fight prices but may worsen unemployment and output losses.

q.q: A final memo says, 'Use policy to stabilize output, but do not ignore expectations.' Why is that good advice?
options: Expectations shift SRAS and SRPC, changing the long-run cost of short-run policy choices.
Expectations only affect M1, so they matter for banking but not inflation or output.
Expectations shift LRAS every time inflation changes, making recessions permanent.
Expectations remove policy lags because people adjust before shocks occur.
q.commonError: Ignoring expectations in stabilization policy.
q.feedback: Expectations affect wage-setting, SRAS, SRPC, inflation persistence, and the cost of disinflation. That is where the bodies are buried.

q.q: Which statement best links an AD expansion to the Phillips curve in the short run?
options: AD rises, output rises, unemployment falls, inflation rises
AD rises, output falls, unemployment rises, inflation falls
AD falls, output rises, unemployment falls, inflation rises
AD falls, output falls, unemployment falls, inflation rises
q.commonError: Breaking the AD-AS to Phillips curve mapping.
q.feedback: Expansionary AD raises output and inflation, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation on SRPC.

q.q: Which statement best links an adverse supply shock across models?
options: SRAS shifts left and SRPC shifts up-right
SRAS shifts right and SRPC shifts down-left
AD shifts right and SRPC shifts down-left
LRAS shifts right and LRPC shifts right
q.commonError: Missing the supply-shock connection across graphs.
q.feedback: An adverse supply shock raises prices, lowers output, and worsens the Phillips curve tradeoff.

q.q: A central bank accommodates an adverse supply shock with more AD. What is the likely tradeoff?
options: Output loss may shrink but inflation rises more
Inflation falls and unemployment rises less
SRAS shifts right and prices fall
LRPC shifts left and inflation vanishes
q.commonError: Thinking accommodation has no inflation cost.
q.feedback: Accommodation can support output but usually worsens inflation pressure.

q.q: A central bank refuses to accommodate an adverse supply shock. What is the likely tradeoff?
options: Inflation pressure is restrained but output loss remains
Output rises and inflation disappears
Unemployment falls and prices fall
SRAS shifts right immediately
q.commonError: Thinking non-accommodation avoids all costs.
q.feedback: Not accommodating helps restrain inflation, but the economy still suffers lower output and higher unemployment.

q.q: A recession lowers output below potential and inflation also falls. Which model pairing fits?
options: AD shifts left and movement down-right on SRPC
SRAS shifts left and SRPC shifts up-right
AD shifts right and movement up-left on SRPC
LRAS shifts right and LRPC shifts right
q.commonError: Confusing demand recessions with supply shocks.
q.feedback: A negative AD shock lowers output and prices, mapping to higher unemployment and lower inflation.

q.q: A boom raises output above potential and inflation rises. Which model pairing fits?
options: AD shifts right and movement up-left on SRPC
SRAS shifts left and SRPC shifts up-right
AD shifts left and movement down-right on SRPC
LRAS shifts left and LRPC shifts right
q.commonError: Missing the short-run AD-to-PC connection.
q.feedback: A positive AD shock raises output and inflation, mapping to lower unemployment and higher inflation.

q.q: In the short run, how does a demand expansion affect output, unemployment and inflation in the AD-AS and Phillips-curve models?
options: AD shifts right; output rises; unemployment falls; inflation rises
AD shifts left; output rises; unemployment falls; inflation falls
SRAS shifts left; output rises; unemployment falls; inflation falls
LRAS shifts right; unemployment rises; inflation rises
q.commonError: Breaking the AD-AS and Phillips curve connection.
q.feedback: A demand expansion raises output and inflation in AD-AS, which maps to lower unemployment and higher inflation on the SRPC.

q.q: A national-security concern applies to one narrowly defined input. Which policy is most economically targeted?
options: A focused resilience policy for that input rather than broad protection across unrelated goods
A tariff on every imported good
A permanent quota on all consumer goods
No comparison of alternatives
q.commonError: ignores_efficiency_or_distribution_evidence
q.feedback: Targeting reduces collateral costs while addressing the stated risk.

q.q: Why is the tariff production-side deadweight loss a social loss?
options: Domestic firms receive revenue
Consumers buy imported goods
The government collects tariff revenue
Higher-cost domestic units replace lower-cost imported units
q.commonError: misses_high_cost_domestic_expansion
q.feedback: The resource cost rises for units shifted to less efficient domestic production.

q.q: Why is the tariff consumption-side deadweight loss a social loss?
options: Consumers stop buying units valued above the world resource cost
Domestic firms sell more units
Government revenue rises
All imported units disappear
q.commonError: misses_lost_low_cost_import_consumption
q.feedback: The tariff prevents mutually beneficial consumption.

q.q: An import quota is administered by first-come, first-served licenses. What additional concern arises?
options: The quota cannot bind
License allocation may reward speed or connections rather than lowest distribution cost
Consumers receive all rents automatically
Domestic price must equal zero
q.commonError: assigns_quota_rents_to_government_automatically
q.feedback: Administrative allocation can create inefficiency and rent-seeking.

q.q: Which statement correctly treats potential compensation from trade?
options: Losers are automatically compensated through prices
Gains can fund compensation, but policy must deliver it.
Potential compensation proves no one loses
Compensation is impossible whenever trade raises total surplus
q.commonError: equates_efficiency_with_fairness
q.feedback: A Kaldor-Hicks gain does not itself transfer resources.

q.q: Which statement about a trade deficit is economically valid?
options: It does not by itself measure whether individual trades create gains from exchange
It proves imports have zero consumer value
It proves every domestic industry is shrinking
It equals tariff deadweight loss
q.commonError: accepts_claim_without_tracing_market_effects
q.feedback: The trade balance is not the surplus test for a particular market.

q.q: A quota-holder spends resources lobbying to obtain import rights. How does rent seeking affect welfare?
options: It turns all rents into consumer surplus
It can dissipate some quota rents and create additional social cost
It removes the domestic price increase
It guarantees efficient license allocation
q.commonError: ignores_efficiency_or_distribution_evidence
q.feedback: Resources spent capturing rents can add to the policy cost.

q.q: Which comparison best tests whether protection is the least-cost response to worker displacement?
options: Compare it with wage insurance, retraining, mobility aid, and targeted income support
Compare only protected-firm profits
Compare only import quantity before and after
Assume no alternative policies exist
q.commonError: ignores_efficiency_or_distribution_evidence
q.feedback: Adjustment goals can be pursued through policies with different efficiency costs.

q.q: A politician says, “Imports destroy domestic production, so imports destroy value.” What is the best response?
options: Imports can lower domestic production, and that loss of domestic output by itself establishes that national welfare falls
Domestic production creates value for the country, whereas imported consumption contributes little to domestic consumer surplus
Imports create net value when the imported quantity is smaller than the domestic production displaced by trade
Imports replace domestic units whose marginal cost exceeds the world price while expanding consumption valued above that price
q.commonError: accepts_claim_without_tracing_market_effects
q.feedback: The welfare gain comes from lower-cost sourcing and additional mutually beneficial consumption.

q.q: A politician says, “Exports make the country poorer because goods leave.” What is the best response?
options: Exports move units to buyers willing to pay the higher world price, raising producer and total surplus despite domestic consumer losses
Exports raise the domestic price, so producer gains are offset dollar-for-dollar by losses to domestic consumers
Exports shift goods abroad without changing domestic willingness to pay or opportunity cost, leaving welfare unchanged
Because residents consume fewer units after trade, the country's welfare falls despite the higher world price
q.commonError: accepts_claim_without_tracing_market_effects
q.feedback: Export welfare analysis compares valuations and costs, not just physical flows.

q.q: A tariff preserves 2,000 jobs in one sector but raises input costs in downstream firms. What analysis is still required?
options: The protected-sector employment effect should be compared with consumer costs, while downstream employment can be treated as secondary
Tariff revenue and protected-sector payroll provide enough information to determine whether the policy raises national welfare
Net employment, consumer costs, fiscal effects, retaliation, and alternative adjustment policies
The job count settles the welfare question once the preserved positions are valued at their current wage payments
q.commonError: treats_policy_slogan_as_complete_analysis
q.feedback: Concentrated benefits do not erase dispersed costs.

q.q: Why can a bilateral tariff reduce the protected country’s exports?
options: Foreign retaliation reduces imports into the protected country while higher input prices raise its exporters’ productivity.
The tariff directly taxes domestic export sales while retaliation lowers the world price of every protected input.
Reduced imports mechanically require equal export losses in each industry while input costs remain unchanged.
Foreign retaliation can reduce market access while tariffed inputs raise domestic exporters’ costs.
q.commonError: treats_policy_slogan_as_complete_analysis
q.feedback: Exports can fall through retaliatory barriers abroad and higher costs of imported inputs at home. Neither an industry-by-industry identity nor direct taxation of exports is required.

q.q: A country is large enough that its import tariff could affect the world price. What should an analyst do?
options: Assume the world price must rise by the full tariff
Ignore the assumption because tariffs never affect foreign prices
State that foreign-price effects require a large-country model rather than silently using the small-country result
Treat tariff revenue as foreign surplus
q.commonError: ignores_price_taking_assumption
q.feedback: Model conclusions depend on maintained assumptions.

q.q: A tariff is removed gradually rather than immediately. Which tradeoff is most relevant?
options: A slower phaseout accelerates consumer gains but concentrates all employment adjustment into the first year.
A slower phaseout preserves tariff revenue without delaying efficiency gains because the announced endpoint is unchanged.
A slower phaseout can ease short-run adjustment but prolong higher prices and distortions relative to immediate removal.
A slower phaseout removes distributional losses by spreading them across years, leaving only consumer gains to compare.
q.commonError: equates_efficiency_with_fairness
q.feedback: Timing affects adjustment capacity as well as how long tariffs distort prices and quantities. Gradual removal can soften disruption while delaying gains; it does not erase distributional losses.

q.q: A tariff raises domestic producer surplus but lowers total surplus. Why are these statements consistent?
options: Producer surplus sits outside total surplus, so producer gains and national welfare can move in opposite directions
Consumer losses are fully captured by producer gains, leaving tariff revenue as the source of deadweight loss
Government revenue reduces total surplus dollar-for-dollar even when the revenue is transferred within the country
Producer gains are a transfer from consumers, while additional consumption and production distortions destroy surplus
q.commonError: counts_transfers_as_social_losses
q.feedback: Transfers and net losses must be separated.

q.q: Arden imposes an $8 tariff and imports 24 units after the tariff. Calculate tariff revenue.
q.commonError: confuses_revenue_with_deadweight_loss
q.feedback: Revenue is $8×24=$192.

q.q: Bellora imposes a $10 tariff and imports 16 units after the tariff. Calculate tariff revenue.
q.commonError: confuses_revenue_with_deadweight_loss
q.feedback: Revenue is $10×16=$160.

q.q: In Arden, an $8 tariff raises domestic production from 10 to 18. Calculate the production-side deadweight loss.
q.commonError: misses_high_cost_domestic_expansion
q.feedback: The triangle is ½×$8×8=$32.

q.q: In Bellora, a $10 tariff raises domestic production from 16 to 26. Calculate the production-side deadweight loss.
q.commonError: misses_high_cost_domestic_expansion
q.feedback: The triangle is ½×$10×10=$50.

q.q: An $8 tariff reduces domestic consumption from 50 to 42. Calculate the consumption-side deadweight loss.
q.commonError: misses_lost_low_cost_import_consumption
q.feedback: The triangle is ½×$8×8=$32.

q.q: A binding quota permits 24 imports and creates a $7 price gap. Calculate total quota rent.
q.commonError: assigns_quota_rents_to_government_automatically
q.feedback: Quota rent is $7×24=$168.

q.q: Refer to the tariff-regions graph. An analyst counts rectangle B as deadweight loss and excludes the two side triangles. Which correction uses the plotted quantities and prices?
options: B is $400 of revenue; the two $100 side triangles total $200 of deadweight loss.
B is $200 of deadweight loss; the side triangles are domestic producer transfers.
B is $200 of revenue; the two $50 side triangles total $100 of deadweight loss.
B is $100 of revenue; the two side triangles total $200 of deadweight loss.
q.commonError: confuses_revenue_with_deadweight_loss
q.feedback: The wedge is 40-30=10 and post-tariff imports are 40-20=20, so B=200. Each distortion base is 10 units, giving 0.5×10×10=50 on each side. Domestic revenue is a transfer; the distortion triangles sum to 100.

q.q: A student says abundant domestic supply automatically makes a country an exporter. What is missing?
options: Domestic demand must be zero
A tariff must be imposed
The country must ban imports
The world price must be above the domestic no-trade equilibrium price
q.commonError: uses_high_supply_instead_of_world_price_comparison
q.feedback: Export status depends on the world-price comparison.

q.q: Private saving is $420 billion, public saving is −$80 billion, and domestic investment is $390 billion. What follows?
options: National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are $50 billion
National saving is −$50 billion, so NCO and NX are −$390 billion
National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are −$50 billion
National saving is $500 billion, so NCO and NX are $110 billion
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving is $340 billion, so NCO and NX are $50 billion” in this international transactions and identities task.
q.feedback: National saving is $420 billion − $80 billion = $340 billion. Subtracting $390 billion of investment gives NCO = NX = −$50 billion.

q.q: A student says a trade deficit proves imports destroyed an equal amount of domestic output. Which correction is best?
options: The deficit proves national saving exceeds domestic investment
The deficit records imports above exports; it does not identify the separate response of domestic production
The claim is correct because imports are subtracted from GDP
A trade deficit means domestic consumption must be falling
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The deficit proves national saving exceeds domestic investment” in this international transactions and identities task.
q.feedback: Imports are subtracted to exclude foreign production from GDP. The trade balance alone does not show how domestic output changed.

q.q: A country has positive NCO but a reported trade deficit. Within the same consistently measured period, which statement is correct?
options: At least one reported balance is inconsistent with the accounting identity
The combination is expected whenever saving is high
Positive NCO mechanically creates a trade deficit
The signs can differ whenever exchange rates float
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The combination is expected whenever saving is high” in this international transactions and identities task.
q.feedback: The identity NX = NCO requires the two balances to share the same value and sign.

q.q: National saving exceeds domestic investment. How does that fact connect to the foreign-exchange market?
options: The saving gap raises demand for domestic currency through imports
Positive NCO removes domestic currency from exchange markets
The saving gap fixes the nominal exchange rate
The positive NCO supplies domestic currency as residents acquire foreign assets
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The saving gap raises demand for domestic currency through imports” in this international transactions and identities task.
q.feedback: S − I is positive NCO. Residents exchange domestic currency to purchase foreign assets, creating foreign-exchange supply.

q.commonError: Forgetting that a binding wage floor creates a surplus when labor supplied exceeds labor demanded.
q.q: A binding minimum wage raises hourly pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces low-skill employment. What is the strongest economic interpretation?
options: Higher wages for some, fewer opportunities for others
The policy must help every worker equally
The policy eliminates structural unemployment
The policy has no effect if firms dislike it
q.feedback: A binding wage floor can raise wages for some workers while creating a labor surplus.

q.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
q.q: Unemployment insurance increases from 12 weeks to 40 weeks. What is the likely tradeoff?
options: Better income protection, but longer searches and more frictional unemployment
Lower income protection and shorter unemployment spells only
Immediate elimination of structural unemployment
A guaranteed fall in labor force participation to zero
q.feedback: Unemployment insurance helps workers smooth income but can reduce urgency to accept work quickly.

q.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
q.q: A recession increases layoffs, while unemployment insurance helps workers avoid immediate hardship but lengthens some searches. Which pair of concepts is involved?
options: Cyclical unemployment and frictional unemployment incentives
Only structural unemployment
GDP deflator and CPI
Natural resources and capital deepening
q.feedback: The recession creates cyclical unemployment; unemployment insurance affects job-search incentives.

q.commonError: Confusing normal job search with skill mismatch or recession layoffs.
q.q: A state increases unemployment benefits but also improves job-placement services. What is the most careful prediction?
options: Benefits slow search; placement services speed it
Frictional unemployment must rise
Frictional unemployment must fall
Only structural unemployment can change
q.feedback: Two forces move in opposite directions, so the net effect is not automatic.

q.commonError: Assuming higher GDP automatically means higher overall well-being.
q.q: Which scenario best shows why GDP per person is more useful than total GDP for comparing living standards?
options: A country’s total GDP rises while its population remains unchanged
A country’s real GDP per person rises while total GDP remains fixed
A country’s GDP doubles while its population triples
A country’s GDP and population both double over the same period
q.feedback: If population grows faster than GDP, average income may fall even though total GDP rises.

q.q: Pollution causes more medical and cleanup spending, raising measured output. Why can the welfare conclusion differ from the GDP change?
options: Medical and cleanup services are excluded whenever pollution caused the demand
GDP subtracts the environmental damage and then subtracts cleanup spending again
Any increase in measured cleanup output proves the original damage improved welfare
GDP counts the services produced but not the full damage that made them necessary
q.commonError: Assumes higher measured production automatically settles the welfare comparison.
q.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

q.q: Workers choose shorter workweeks, measured output falls, and leisure rises. Which inference is justified?
options: GDP stays unchanged because added leisure replaces every lost unit of production
The leisure gain is automatically valued and added to business investment
GDP falls, but well-being could rise or fall
Both measured GDP and total well-being must decline by the same amount
q.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
q.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

q.q: A storm destroys productive assets, followed by a surge in rebuilding services. What distinction is essential?
options: Higher rebuilding output proves the storm created a net gain for every household
Current production can rise while lost wealth and hardship leave welfare lower
Rebuilding services cannot enter GDP because the storm destroyed assets first
The destroyed productive assets are added to current household consumption spending
q.commonError: Treats GDP as either a complete welfare index or a useless statistic.
q.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

q.q: If the price level rises, what happens in the money market under the interest-rate effect?
options: Money demand rises, interest rates rise, and investment falls.
Money demand falls, interest rates fall, and investment rises.
Money supply rises, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
Money demand rises, interest rates fall, and investment rises.
q.commonError: reversing the price-level money-demand relationship
q.feedback: Higher prices increase money demand, which raises interest rates and reduces investment.

q.q: Why does a lower price level increase the quantity of goods and services demanded?
options: Lower prices reduce money demand, lower interest rates, and increase investment.
Lower prices increase money demand, raise interest rates, and lower investment.
Lower prices reduce money supply and shift AD left.
Lower prices eliminate the need for investment.
q.commonError: thinking lower prices raise money demand
q.feedback: Lower prices reduce money demand, which lowers interest rates and raises investment spending.

q.q: If income rises and the Fed prevents interest rates from rising, what policy shift is needed?
options: Increase money supply as money demand rises
Decrease money supply as money demand rises
Increase money demand as money supply falls
Decrease money demand as interest rates rise
q.commonError: Forgetting the Fed must offset higher money demand.
q.feedback: Higher income raises money demand; to hold rates down, the Fed must increase money supply.

q.q: If the Fed cuts money supply while money demand rises, what happens to the interest rate pressure?
options: It rises from both forces
It falls from both forces
It rises from supply but falls from demand
It falls from supply but rises from demand
q.commonError: Missing that both shifts raise rates.
q.feedback: Lower money supply and higher money demand both push the interest rate upward.

q.q: Money demand increases while the money supply remains fixed. What is the likely effect on the interest rate and interest-sensitive investment?
options: r rises and investment falls.
r falls and investment rises.
r rises and investment rises.
r falls and investment falls.
q.commonError: thinking higher money demand lowers the interest rate
q.feedback: With fixed money supply, a rightward shift in money demand raises the interest rate, which lowers investment.

q.q: Money demand shifts left while money supply remains fixed. What chain follows?
options: r falls, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
r rises, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
r falls, investment falls, and AD tends to decrease.
r rises, investment rises, and AD tends to increase.
q.commonError: missing the investment response after the money-market movement
q.feedback: Lower money demand reduces the equilibrium interest rate, which supports investment and AD.

q.q: If an increase in Y raises money demand and the Fed wants to prevent r from rising, what should the Fed do?
options: Increase money supply to match the higher money demand.
Decrease money supply to reduce money demand.
Raise taxes because money supply cannot shift.
Reduce government spending to make MD vertical.
q.commonError: thinking the Fed should reduce money supply when money demand rises
q.feedback: If money demand rises, increasing money supply can prevent the equilibrium interest rate from rising.

q.q: Income rises, money demand shifts right, and the Fed holds money supply fixed. What memo is strongest?
options: Interest rates rise unless the Fed increases money supply.
Interest rates fall because higher income lowers money demand.
Interest rates stay fixed because money demand cannot shift.
Interest rates fall because fixed money supply means more lending.
q.commonError: Reversing income effects on money demand.
q.feedback: Higher income raises money demand; with fixed money supply, interest rates rise.

q.q: Money demand rises because income rises, while the Fed cuts the money supply. Which memo is strongest?
options: Both forces push interest rates upward and pressure AD downward.
Both forces push interest rates downward and pressure AD upward.
Money demand raises rates, but lower money supply lowers rates.
Money demand lowers rates, but lower money supply raises rates.
q.commonError: Missing that both shifts raise interest rates.
q.feedback: Higher money demand and lower money supply both raise interest rates, weakening investment and AD.

q.q: Money demand falls while the Fed expands money supply. Which memo is strongest?
options: Both forces push interest rates downward and support AD.
Both forces push interest rates upward and weaken AD.
Money demand lowers rates, but higher money supply raises rates.
Money demand raises rates, but higher money supply lowers rates.
q.commonError: Missing that both shifts lower interest rates.
q.feedback: Lower money demand and higher money supply both push interest rates down, supporting investment and AD.

q.q: Starting in money-market equilibrium, the price level rises. Which full chain explains the interest-rate effect on aggregate demand?
options: Higher P raises money demand, raises r, lowers investment, and lowers quantity of goods and services demanded.
Higher P lowers money demand, lowers r, raises investment, and raises quantity demanded.
Higher P raises money supply, lowers r, raises investment, and shifts AD right.
Higher P lowers money supply, raises r, and shifts money demand left.
q.commonError: reversing the price-level effect on money demand
q.feedback: Higher prices require more money for transactions. That raises money demand, raises interest rates, lowers investment, and reduces quantity demanded.

q.q: Starting at P1 and r1, the price level falls to P2. What happens in the money market and AD model?
options: Money demand falls, r falls, investment rises, and output demanded rises.
Money demand rises, r rises, investment falls, and output demanded falls.
Money supply falls, r rises, and AD shifts left.
Money demand falls, r rises, and investment falls.
q.commonError: thinking lower prices increase money demand
q.feedback: A lower price level reduces money demand, lowers interest rates, raises investment, and increases quantity demanded.

q.q: Money demand rises while the Fed increases money supply. Which conclusion is safest?
options: Higher money demand pushes the rate down and higher supply pushes it down; the effects reinforce
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it down; opposite directions ensure an unchanged rate
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it down; relative shifts determine the result
Higher money demand pushes the rate up and higher supply pushes it up; the effects reinforce
q.commonError: Assuming one shift always dominates.
q.feedback: When money demand and money supply both increase, the interest-rate effect depends on which shift is larger.

q.q: Money demand and supply both rise. The interest rate is unchanged. Which inference is justified?
options: The schedules stayed fixed; an unchanged rate rules out either schedule changing.
The shifts offset at the observed rate; both schedules can have changed.
Demand fell as supply rose; opposite quantity shifts preserve the observed rate.
Income and prices stayed fixed; an unchanged rate establishes both underlying variables.
q.commonError: Incorrect inference: The schedules stayed fixed; an unchanged rate rules out either schedule changing.
q.feedback: Equal demand and supply additions at the same rate can leave the rate fixed. An unchanged equilibrium price does not identify unchanged underlying schedules.

q.commonError: Comparing total GDP instead of output per person.
q.q: A poor country grows quickly after gaining stable property rights, schools, and foreign investment. Which explanation is strongest?
options: Catch-up potential plus growth-supporting institutions
Growth must be caused only by inflation
Poor countries grow automatically regardless of policy
Property rights reduce investment
q.feedback: Catch-up growth is more likely when institutions support investment, human capital, and technology adoption.

q.q: Real GDP per person rises, but average leisure falls sharply and pollution worsens. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Market output per person rose, but overall well-being may have changed differently.
Living standards rose by exactly the same rate because GDP per person captures all welfare changes.
GDP per person becomes unusable whenever leisure or environmental quality changes.
Pollution and lost leisure are already fully subtracted from measured real GDP.
q.commonError: Treating real GDP per person as a complete measure of welfare.
q.feedback: Real GDP per person is useful for material output, but it does not fully capture leisure, environmental quality, distribution, or nonmarket activity.

q.q: Real GDP is initially $250 billion. It grows 6%, while population grows 8%. Which statement reconciles aggregate growth and average output?
options: Aggregate output falls because population growth exceeds GDP growth
Aggregate real output rises, but real GDP per person falls about 1.9%
Both aggregate and per-person real output rise 6%
Per-person output rises 14% because output and population growth add
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Aggregate output falls because population growth exceeds GDP growth” in this living standards and growth task.
q.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.06/1.08−1≈−1.85%. A larger economy can have lower average output if population grows faster.

q.q: Real GDP is initially $100 billion. It grows 6%, while population grows 8%. Which statement reconciles aggregate growth and average output?
options: Aggregate real output rises, but real GDP per person falls about 1.9%
Both aggregate and per-person real output rise 6%
Per-person output rises 14% because output and population growth add
Aggregate output falls because population growth exceeds GDP growth
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both aggregate and per-person real output rise 6%” in this living standards and growth task.
q.feedback: Per-person output changes by 1.06/1.08−1≈−1.85%. A larger economy can have lower average output if population grows faster.

q.q: A larger budget deficit lowers public saving while private-saving behavior and investment determinants remain unchanged. Which complete loanable-funds sequence follows?
options: National saving falls, investment demand shifts left, and both the rate and quantity fall
National saving rises, supply shifts right, and investment falls along demand
National saving is unchanged because public saving is not part of loanable-funds supply
Supply shifts left, raising the rate and reducing investment
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving falls, investment demand shifts left, and both the rate and quantity fall” in this loanable funds equilibrium task.
q.feedback: Public saving is part of national saving, which supplies loanable funds. A deficit lowers that supply, raises the equilibrium real interest rate, and crowds out investment along unchanged demand.

q.q: The real interest rate and equilibrium quantity both fall while saving supply is unchanged. Which explanation is most consistent with those observations?
options: Households became more willing to save at every real rate
Weaker expected sales reduced investment demand at every real rate
A larger deficit reduced public and national saving
The lower real rate caused investment demand to shift left
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Households became more willing to save at every real rate” in this loanable funds shifts task.
q.feedback: With supply fixed, a leftward investment-demand shift lowers both equilibrium variables. Weaker sales expectations provide the causal determinant; the rate change itself produces movement along demand.

q.q: Technology improves expected project returns, but the equilibrium real interest rate subsequently rises. Which statement correctly separates the two effects on investment?
options: Technology moves firms along demand, while the higher rate shifts the entire curve left
Both changes shift demand right because equilibrium investment initially rises
The higher rate shifts loanable-funds supply left and leaves investment demand unchanged
Demand shifts right; the higher rate partly offsets the increase
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Technology moves firms along demand, while the higher rate shifts the entire curve left” in this loanable funds shifts task.
q.feedback: Improved technology changes profitability at every rate and shifts investment demand right. The endogenous rate increase makes fewer marginal projects profitable along the new curve, partly offsetting the initial increase.

q.q: A deficit lowers saving while new technology raises investment demand. What can be concluded without shift magnitudes?
options: Saving supply shifts left and investment demand right; the rate rises while quantity depends on relative shifts
Saving supply shifts left and investment demand right; quantity rises while the rate depends on relative shifts
Saving supply shifts right and investment demand right; quantity rises while the rate depends on relative shifts
Saving supply shifts left and investment demand left; quantity falls while the rate depends on relative shifts
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Saving supply shifts left and investment demand right; quantity rises while the rate depends on relative shifts” in this loanable funds shifts task.
q.feedback: Supply left and demand right both raise the rate, but they push equilibrium quantity in opposite directions.

q.q: Expected investment profitability falls while a budget deficit also reduces national saving. What must happen, and what remains uncertain?
options: The real rate falls, while equilibrium quantity is ambiguous
Quantity falls; the real-rate direction is ambiguous
Both the real rate and quantity must rise
The real rate must remain unchanged, while quantity falls
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The real rate falls, while equilibrium quantity is ambiguous” in this loanable funds shifts task.
q.feedback: Investment demand shifts left and loanable-funds supply shifts left. Both changes reduce equilibrium quantity, but demand puts downward pressure on the rate while supply puts upward pressure on it.

q.q: A productivity improvement lowers production costs and raises potential output over time. Which curves are most likely affected?
options: SRAS right and LRAS right
AD left and SRAS left
SRPC up and AD left
MD right and MS left
q.commonError: Treating productivity only as demand.
q.feedback: Higher productivity can shift SRAS right and increase long-run aggregate supply.

q.q: A permanent tax credit raises capital investment, while a temporary wage subsidy lowers current labor costs. Which supply changes are most likely?
options: LRAS shifts right over time and SRAS shifts right immediately.
SRAS shifts left because subsidies raise wages
LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
Only AD shifts right
q.commonError: Failing to distinguish capacity growth from current cost reduction.
q.feedback: More capital raises potential output, while the subsidy lowers short-run production cost.

q.q: A country receives a permanent productivity improvement and a temporary spike in imported input prices. Which graph change best fits?
options: Both curves shift left permanently
LRAS shifts left and SRAS right
Only aggregate demand shifts
LRAS shifts right, while SRAS may shift left initially.
q.commonError: Failing to separate permanent capacity from temporary production costs.
q.feedback: Productivity raises potential output; costly imported inputs can reduce short-run supply.

q.q: A permanent improvement in education raises worker productivity, but a new regulation raises current compliance costs. Which statement is most complete?
options: LRAS shifts right; opposing SRAS effects make its net shift uncertain
LRAS shifts left; both changes move SRAS to the left
LRAS is unchanged; both changes move SRAS to the right
LRAS shifts right; compliance costs necessarily outweigh productivity gains
q.commonError: Treating permanent productivity and current cost changes as identical.
q.feedback: Education raises capacity; compliance costs can reduce short-run supply.

q.q: Capital is destroyed while a new technology raises productivity. Which LRAS conclusion is valid?
options: Capital loss reduces capacity and technology raises it; net LRAS direction requires relative effects
Capital loss reduces capacity and technology raises it; opposite effects establish unchanged LRAS
Capital loss reduces capacity and technology affects only current costs; LRAS shifts left
Technology raises capacity and capital loss affects only current costs; LRAS shifts right
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Capital loss reduces capacity and technology raises it; opposite effects establish unchanged LRAS” in this long run aggregate supply and potential output task.
q.feedback: Lost capital and better technology push potential output in opposite directions.

q.q: A negative AD shock lowers output and prices. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
options: Wages and expected prices fall
Wages and expected prices rise
Money demand rises permanently
LRPC shifts right
q.commonError: Thinking recessionary gaps cannot self-correct.
q.feedback: Lower wages and expected prices shift SRAS right and help output return to natural.

q.q: A positive AD shock pushes output above potential. What long-run adjustment restores output if no policy responds?
options: Wages and expected prices rise
Wages and expected prices fall
SRAS shifts right immediately
LRAS shifts to AD2
q.commonError: Thinking booms above potential persist forever.
q.feedback: Higher wages and expected prices shift SRAS left and return output to potential.

q.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD rises unexpectedly, then expected prices rise. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Prices fall first, then AD shifts left
LRAS shifts right, then output falls
q.commonError: Skipping the short-run expansion before long-run adjustment.
q.feedback: An unexpected AD increase raises output in the short run, but higher expected prices later shift SRAS left.

q.q: An economy begins at natural output. AD falls unexpectedly, then expected prices fall. Which sequence is most likely?
options: Output falls first, then SRAS shifts right
Output rises first, then SRAS shifts left
Prices rise first, then LRAS shifts left
AD rises first, then unemployment rises
q.commonError: Skipping the short-run recession before self-correction.
q.feedback: An unexpected AD decrease lowers output first, then lower expected prices shift SRAS right over time.

q.q: Inflation rises permanently after repeated demand expansion, but labor-market structure is unchanged. Which long-run statement is strongest?
options: Unemployment remains permanently below natural after expectations fully adjust
The LRPC shifts right because the price level rose over time
Unemployment returns toward the same natural rate on an unchanged LRPC
The LRPC shifts left because higher inflation permanently improves job matching
q.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
q.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

q.q: The natural rate falls because job search becomes faster. How should SRPC and LRPC reasoning be separated?
options: LRPC stays fixed while unemployment permanently departs from its vertical location
LRPC shifts left; short-run curves may also reposition around the new natural rate
The economy merely moves upward along the old LRPC as inflation changes
Only inflation expectations can shift LRPC in the long-run model
q.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
q.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

q.q: Economy A lowers its natural rate through better job matching; Economy B only creates an unexpected demand boom. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both economies permanently shift LRPC left because unemployment initially declines
Only Economy B changes long-run unemployment by raising aggregate demand
Neither economy can affect unemployment at either a short or long horizon
A can shift LRPC left; B can only move unemployment below natural temporarily
q.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
q.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

q.q: Inflation expectations instantly match a fully anticipated monetary expansion in the model. What Phillips prediction is most consistent?
options: A rightward LRPC shift from higher money growth and unchanged labor institutions
A guaranteed fall in both inflation and unemployment after expectations adjust
Little or no temporary unemployment movement away from the natural rate
A permanent unemployment decline along the SRPC once nominal spending increases
q.commonError: Infers a permanent unemployment gain from the downward-sloping SRPC.
q.feedback: The LRPC is vertical at the natural rate because expected inflation adjusts in the long run.

q.q: A government insists on holding unemployment below the natural rate after inflation expectations have adjusted. What does the long-run Phillips-curve model predict?
options: A stable inflation rate will permanently sustain lower unemployment.
The policy requires continuously accelerating inflation.
Unemployment will fall to zero without further inflation.
The natural rate automatically falls whenever aggregate demand rises.
q.commonError: Believing a stable higher inflation rate buys a permanent unemployment reduction.
q.feedback: Once expected inflation catches up, maintaining below-natural unemployment requires repeated new inflation surprises.

q.q: A labor-market reform lowers the natural rate while a demand expansion temporarily lowers unemployment even further. Which distinction is essential?
options: Demand shifts LRPC permanently while reform only changes the current inflation rate
Neither change can alter a Phillips curve once expectations are specified
The reform shifts LRPC; the demand expansion creates temporary movement relative to it
Both changes are movements along one unchanged SRPC despite different mechanisms
q.commonError: Moves the economy along a fixed LRPC when the natural rate changes.
q.feedback: A change in labor-market structure can shift the vertical LRPC to a new natural rate.

q.q: Demand increases while supply decreases, and the observed equilibrium quantity is unchanged. Which inference best reconciles the two shifts with that observation?
options: Equilibrium price rises, and the opposing quantity effects happen to offset
Equilibrium price falls, and the two shifts reinforce the quantity effect
Equilibrium quantity is unchanged because neither curve shifts
Equilibrium price is unchanged because the demand and supply shifts are equal
q.commonError: claims_quantity_change_is_certain_in_opposing_shifts
q.feedback: A demand increase and supply decrease both raise equilibrium price. Their quantity effects oppose one another, and the observed unchanged quantity indicates that those effects offset in this case.

q.q: Demand decreases while supply increases. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium quantity falls
q.commonError: claims_quantity_change_is_certain_in_opposing_shifts
q.feedback: Both shifts push price down, but quantity is ambiguous.

q.q: Demand and supply both increase. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity falls
q.commonError: claims_price_change_is_certain_when_both_curves_shift_right
q.feedback: Both shifts increase quantity, but price depends on which shift is larger.

q.q: Demand and supply both decrease. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium price falls
Equilibrium quantity rises
q.commonError: claims_price_change_is_certain_when_both_curves_shift_left
q.feedback: Both shifts reduce quantity, but price is ambiguous.

q.q: A market price is above equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
options: Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
No pressure because high prices clear every market
Downward pressure on quantity demanded because demand shifts left
q.commonError: confuses_surplus_with_shortage
q.feedback: A price above equilibrium creates a surplus, so sellers have an incentive to lower price.

q.q: A market price is below equilibrium. What pressure does the market create and why?
options: Upward pressure on price because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
Downward pressure on price because quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
No pressure because buyers prefer low prices
A supply increase because the legal price is low
q.commonError: confuses_shortage_with_surplus
q.feedback: A price below equilibrium creates a shortage, so buyers compete and push price upward.

q.q: Consumer interest in a product falls while new technology lowers production costs. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Price falls, but quantity is ambiguous
Quantity rises, but price is ambiguous
Both price and quantity rise
Both price and quantity fall
q.commonError: assumes_supply_effect_dominates_demand_effect
q.feedback: A demand decrease and supply increase both lower price, but quantity is ambiguous.

q.q: A celebrity endorsement increases demand for a product at the same time input costs rise. What can be predicted with certainty?
options: Equilibrium price rises
Equilibrium quantity rises
Equilibrium quantity falls
Equilibrium price falls
q.commonError: claims_quantity_change_is_certain
q.feedback: Demand rises and supply falls. Both raise price, but quantity is ambiguous.

q.q: Demand and supply both increase. The equilibrium quantity rises, but the equilibrium price is unchanged. What does this reveal?
options: Neither curve shifted because an unchanged price proves the market did not move.
Demand increased more than supply, so price should have risen instead of staying fixed.
The price effects offset, while both shifts raise equilibrium quantity.
Supply decreased while demand increased, creating offsetting quantity effects.
q.commonError: Assuming an unchanged price means the market experienced no shifts.
q.feedback: A demand increase raises price and quantity, while a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Equal price effects can cancel while quantity rises.

q.q: Demand increases while supply decreases. Which equilibrium outcome is certain?
options: The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.
The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.
q.commonError: Claiming certainty about quantity when the two shifts move quantity in opposite directions.
q.feedback: Both shifts raise price, while demand raises quantity and lower supply reduces quantity.

q.q: Both demand and supply shift left in the same market. Which equilibrium result can be stated without knowing the shift sizes?
options: The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.
The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.
q.commonError: Claiming certainty about price when both curves shift left.
q.feedback: Both shifts reduce equilibrium quantity, but their price effects oppose each other.

q.q: A fall in aggregate demand reduces national output, while some firms cut employment more than others. What levels of analysis are present?
options: Only microeconomic analysis because the firms are the ones changing employment.
Macro analysis of the overall contraction and micro analysis of firm responses.
Only macro analysis.
Neither, because both use employment data.
q.commonError: Forcing a mixed question into only one level.
q.feedback: The aggregate shock is macroeconomic; heterogeneous firm choices are microeconomic.

q.q: A tax changes one product’s price and also affects total consumer spending. Why might both fields be needed?
options: The tax eliminates the distinction between fields.
Only macroeconomics is needed because total consumer spending changes.
Macroeconomics studies only government budgets.
Microeconomics studies the product market; macroeconomics studies aggregate spending.
q.commonError: Assuming a policy belongs exclusively to one field.
q.feedback: One event can have market-level and economy-wide consequences.

q.q: A drought reduces one region’s wheat supply and later contributes to national food inflation. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Inflation is always one-market analysis
The event has market-level and aggregate dimensions
Weather makes the question noneconomic
Food prices are always only microeconomic
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

q.q: One factory closes while the national unemployment rate falls. What prevents a contradiction?
options: Macroeconomic data exclude factory workers
Firm closures always raise national employment
A single firm outcome need not match the national aggregate
The unemployment rate describes only one industry
q.commonError: Generalizing a narrow sample directly to the national economy.
q.feedback: Macro conclusions require appropriate aggregation across people, firms, and markets.

q.q: Which research design is most clearly microeconomic despite using a very large dataset?
options: Estimating how individual consumers respond to a change in one product’s price.
Measuring national inflation over time, because all price questions are economy-wide
Explaining long-run growth in real GDP per person.
Forecasting the economy-wide unemployment rate.
q.commonError: Using dataset size rather than unit of analysis.
q.feedback: Microeconomics can use massive data while focusing on individual choices and specific markets.

q.q: Which statement best characterizes the boundary between micro and macro?
options: Microeconomics studies prices and firms, while macroeconomics studies government policy
The distinction concerns the level and aggregation of the question, not an absolute separation of topics.
Any government policy is automatically macroeconomic
Firm-level outcomes cannot contribute to macroeconomic outcomes.
q.commonError: Treating the fields as disconnected topic lists.
q.feedback: Many issues can be studied at both individual-market and aggregate levels.

q.q: A factory replaces workers with equipment. Its investment rises while other firms postpone purchases. Which statement about the evidence is justified?
options: The factory's higher investment establishes a rise in national investment
Postponement elsewhere makes the factory decision a macro question only
Opposite firm responses make national investment impossible to measure
The factory decision is micro; the direction of national investment requires aggregation
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: Individual changes can offset one another. The factory decision and the national total are related but distinct questions.

q.q: Workers relocate from rural districts to a city. City rents and employment rise. Which claim needs additional economy-wide evidence?
options: National employment rose rather than being redistributed across locations
The city's housing market experienced a local change
The move changed some households' location choices
Employers in the city gained access to more workers
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: Local gains can reflect transfers from other locations. National employment must account for origin districts and other responses; city outcomes alone cannot settle it.

q.q: A housing subsidy raises rents locally and changes national construction spending. What is the best approach?
options: Analyze both the market response and aggregate effect
Use macro only because spending is measured
Use micro only because rents change
Treat the two outcomes as unrelated
q.commonError: Forcing a question with market and aggregate consequences into only one field.
q.feedback: One event can require both market-level and economy-wide analysis.

q.q: One industry loses jobs while national employment grows. Which explanation is valid?
options: National employment excludes changes that occur within individual industries.
Sector change can differ from the aggregate
The industry result disproves the aggregate
Job data cannot cross levels
q.commonError: Generalizing a narrow sample directly to the national economy.
q.feedback: Macro conclusions require appropriate aggregation across people, firms, and markets.

q.q: A federal rule applies to a narrowly defined appliance market. What determines its field?
options: The number of pages in the rule
Whether policymakers support it
The outcome and aggregation being studied
The federal source of the rule alone
q.commonError: Classifying by size, institution, or topic word instead of the unit of analysis.
q.feedback: Microeconomics examines households, firms, and particular markets.

q.q: A model fits historical data but fails after institutions change. Which limitation is most relevant?
options: Relationships estimated under old rules may not remain stable.
Historical data can never be useful.
Institutions are outside economics.
Model assumptions matter only for graphs.
q.commonError: Assuming past empirical relationships are invariant.
q.feedback: Institutional change can alter incentives and the parameters of a model.

q.q: A highly detailed model predicts poorly because many parameters are estimated imprecisely. What does this illustrate?
options: Simple models always predict perfectly.
Parameters have no role in models.
More complexity can add noise and does not guarantee better prediction.
Prediction quality depends only on graphics.
q.commonError: Assuming complexity automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: Extra detail can create estimation problems and overfitting.

q.q: A housing model estimated where construction is flexible is applied where zoning is strict. What is the central concern?
options: Zoning makes housing demand irrelevant
A more detailed model must automatically be correct
The supply assumption may not transfer across cities
Historical estimates are always invalid elsewhere
q.commonError: Transferring a result without checking context or omitted factors.
q.feedback: Strict zoning violates the flexible-construction condition, so transferring the housing estimate may produce poor predictions.

q.q: A transit model worked before remote work became common but now overpredicts commuting. What should be reconsidered?
options: Whether any historical data can ever be useful
Whether commuting belongs in economics
Whether assumptions matter only in graphs
Whether the old behavioral relationship remains stable
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: Remote work changed the commuting relationship, so the model’s stability and workplace-attendance assumptions need reassessment.

q.q: A model uses an unrealistic assumption but predicts well in a narrow setting. What is the strongest evaluation?
options: Judge whether the abstraction serves that narrow purpose
Reject the model because every assumption must be literal
Accept the model for all settings without further checks
Treat predictive fit as proof of the assumed mechanism
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: A simplifying assumption need not be literally realistic if the model predicts well for the narrow question and setting in which it is used.

q.q: A complex model predicts purchases accurately, while a simpler model identifies a price mechanism. Which model should be preferred?
options: Always choose the simple model regardless of performance
Average the models because mechanisms cannot be tested
Choose according to whether prediction or explanation is the goal
Always choose the complex model because it has better fit
q.commonError: Choosing by complexity or preference instead of purpose.
q.feedback: Forecast accuracy favors the complex model for prediction, while the simpler model may be better for identifying and communicating the price mechanism.

q.q: A model predicts policy outcomes accurately in several cities, but its proposed mechanism was never measured. What follows?
options: Accurate predictions establish the proposed mechanism locally, though they leave its transfer to other cities uncertain.
Accurate predictions support usefulness in those cities, but competing mechanisms may fit the same outcomes.
Repeated prediction success establishes literal assumptions, though it leaves the mechanism’s policy importance uncertain.
An unmeasured mechanism invalidates the predictions, even if independent outcome data confirm their accuracy.
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: Predictive success is evidence about predictive performance. It does not discriminate between mechanisms that produce the same observable predictions, nor prove every assumption literal.

q.q: Two models fit past data, but only one predicts behavior after a new fee. What evidence best separates them?
options: The recommendation preferred by the policymaker
Evidence from the new fee setting where predictions differ
More past outcomes both models already reproduce
The relative length of the two model descriptions
q.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
q.feedback: The new fee creates an out-of-sample case where the models disagree, so observed post-fee behavior can distinguish them.

q.q: A policy conclusion disappears when one plausible assumption changes. What is the strongest evaluation?
options: The conclusion is sensitive and should be qualified
The original conclusion remains fully robust
The alternate assumption should be hidden from users
The model is useless for every other question
q.commonError: Using the model without checking its purpose, assumptions, or evidence.
q.feedback: A conclusion that disappears under one plausible assumption is fragile and should be reported with that sensitivity clearly stated.

q.q: A larger model fits old data better but predicts new data worse. What does this show?
options: Historical fit proves the larger model is superior
Prediction quality depends only on equation length
The smaller model must omit every relevant mechanism
Added complexity can overfit rather than improve transfer
q.commonError: Assuming additional detail automatically improves a model.
q.feedback: Better historical fit paired with worse new-data prediction is evidence of overfitting rather than a general gain from complexity.

q.q: During a panic, banks hold excess reserves and households withdraw deposits into currency. What happens to the money multiplier?
options: It falls below the simple multiplier prediction.
It rises above the simple multiplier prediction.
It becomes equal to the reserve requirement.
It becomes unrelated to bank behavior.
q.commonError: using the simple multiplier mechanically during financial stress
q.feedback: Both excess reserves and currency withdrawals weaken deposit creation, so the actual multiplier falls.

q.q: A central bank wants to expand lending but banks are already holding large excess reserves. Which issue is most relevant?
options: Bank willingness to lend may limit money creation.
Commodity money must replace fiat money.
M1 must exclude checking deposits.
Velocity must be exactly zero.
q.commonError: thinking more reserves automatically guarantees more loans
q.feedback: More reserves do not guarantee more lending if banks are unwilling to lend.

q.q: A Fed bond purchase increases reserves, but households convert much of the new deposits into currency. What is the likely result?
options: The money supply rises by less than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply rises by more than the simple multiplier predicts.
The money supply cannot rise at all because bonds were purchased.
Currency holdings make the reserve requirement negative.
q.commonError: ignoring leakages from deposits into currency
q.feedback: Currency drain limits redepositing, so the multiplier effect is weaker.

q.q: Which statement best explains why banks cannot make society rich simply by creating more money through lending?
options: Money creation can increase nominal balances, but it does not automatically create real goods and services.
Every bank loan creates new factories instantly.
Money creation permanently increases real output without limits.
The money supply is unrelated to prices or output.
q.commonError: thinking more money means more real wealth automatically
q.feedback: Banks can help create money, but real wealth depends on real goods, services, labor, capital, and productivity.

q.q: The Fed buys bonds during a banking panic, but households increase currency holdings and banks increase excess reserves. What should students infer?
options: Fed control is limited by depositor and bank behavior
The money multiplier must rise to its maximum
Open-market purchases cannot affect reserves
Currency holdings are excluded from M1
q.commonError: Ignoring leakage from currency holdings and excess reserves.
q.feedback: Fed purchases add reserves, but currency withdrawals and excess reserve holdings can weaken money creation.

q.q: Which answer best explains why lowering the discount rate may not create much lending during a crisis?
options: Banks may still avoid borrowing or lending if they see borrowers as too risky.
Lower borrowing costs always force banks to lend.
The discount rate controls tax rates, not bank borrowing.
Lower discount rates automatically create commodity money.
q.commonError: assuming cheaper Fed credit guarantees private lending
q.feedback: Lowering the discount rate helps only if banks are willing to borrow and lend.

q.q: Which statement best combines the simplified deposit-multiplier model with monetary-control limits?
options: Excess reserves and currency holdings weaken deposit multiplication.
Fractional reserve banking guarantees exact Fed control of M1.
The multiplier works only with commodity money.
Currency drain increases bank reserves and expands lending.
q.commonError: thinking the multiplier mechanism is automatic and exact
q.feedback: Fractional-reserve banking can multiply deposits, but excess reserves and currency holdings can make the actual expansion smaller than the simple model predicts.

q.q: A bank has $2 million in assets and $120,000 in capital. If asset values fall by 4 percent, capital falls to:
q.commonError: Applying the loss percentage to capital instead of assets.
q.feedback: A 4 percent asset loss is $80,000, so capital falls from $120,000 to $40,000.

q.q: All nominal prices double except wages, which rise only 50 percent. What happens to real wages?
options: Real wages fall because nominal wages rise less than the price level.
Real wages rise because nominal wages rose.
Real wages are unchanged because all prices rose.
Real wages double because prices doubled.
q.commonError: thinking any nominal wage increase raises the real wage
q.feedback: Real wages depend on wages relative to prices. If wages rise 50 percent while prices double, real wages fall.

q.q: A student says, 'Since money is neutral, monetary policy cannot affect output during recessions.' Which correction is strongest?
options: Neutrality is a long-run claim; short-run sticky prices allow AD effects on output.
Neutrality means money changes output permanently but not prices.
Neutrality applies only to fiscal policy and never to money.
Neutrality means the Phillips curve slopes downward in the long run.
q.commonError: Applying long-run neutrality to every short-run case.
q.feedback: Money is neutral in the long run, but monetary policy can affect output in the short run through aggregate demand.

q.q: Which sequence best describes a contractionary open-market operation?
options: Sell bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Buy bonds, reserves fall, lending weakens
Sell bonds, reserves rise, lending expands
Buy bonds, reserves rise, lending contracts
q.commonError: Reversing bond sales and purchases.
q.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, weakens lending, and reduces money creation.

q.q: The Fed raises the discount rate and also raises interest on reserves. Which combined effect is most likely?
options: Banks borrow less from the Fed and may hold more reserves.
Banks borrow more from the Fed and lend every reserve.
Households automatically hold fewer dollars because taxes fall.
The money multiplier becomes infinite.
q.commonError: treating all Fed tools as expansionary regardless of direction
q.feedback: A higher discount rate discourages bank borrowing, and higher interest on reserves can encourage banks to hold reserves.

q.q: If the Fed wants looser money but also raises interest on reserves, what tension does this create?
options: It injects reserves but may also encourage banks to hold them instead of lending.
It lowers reserves and forces banks to lend more.
It turns deposits into commodity money.
It makes fiscal policy impossible.
q.commonError: assuming all policy tools point in the same direction
q.feedback: More reserves can support lending, but higher interest on reserves may make banks sit on those reserves.

q.q: The Fed buys bonds while also increasing interest on reserves. Which answer best captures the policy conflict?
options: Bond purchases add reserves, but higher interest on reserves may reduce banks' willingness to lend them.
Bond purchases remove reserves, while higher interest on reserves forces banks to lend more.
Both actions clearly reduce reserves and contract lending.
Both actions clearly eliminate money demand.
q.commonError: assuming every Fed action in a scenario pushes the same direction
q.feedback: Buying bonds is expansionary, but higher interest on reserves can make banks hold reserves instead of lending them.

q.q: Which policy package most strongly reduces bank lending capacity?
options: Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed buys bonds and lowers the discount rate.
Fed lowers reserve requirements and buys bonds.
q.commonError: failing to combine multiple contractionary tools
q.feedback: Selling bonds drains reserves, higher reserve requirements restrict lending, and higher interest on reserves encourages banks to hold reserves.

q.q: Which policy package most strongly expands bank lending capacity?
options: Fed buys bonds, lowers reserve requirements, and lowers interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds, raises reserve requirements, and raises interest on reserves.
Fed sells bonds and raises the discount rate.
Fed raises reserve requirements and pays banks more to hold reserves.
q.commonError: missing that lower interest on reserves can encourage lending
q.feedback: Buying bonds adds reserves, lower reserve requirements free reserves, and lower interest on reserves weakens the incentive to sit on reserves.

q.q: The Fed cuts the discount rate, buys bonds, and lowers interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Bank borrowing and reserves rise, lending incentives strengthen, and the money supply tends to expand.
Bank reserves fall, lending incentives weaken, and the money supply contracts.
Taxes fall, consumption rises, and fiscal policy expands.
The money supply is unaffected because only fiscal policy matters.
q.commonError: treating Fed tools as unrelated one-off facts
q.feedback: All three actions push toward monetary expansion: cheaper Fed borrowing, more reserves, and less reward for holding reserves idle.

q.q: The Fed raises the discount rate, sells bonds, and raises interest on reserves. What is the most complete expected effect?
options: Borrowing becomes costlier, reserves fall, banks may hold more reserves, and money creation weakens.
Borrowing becomes cheaper, reserves rise, and lending expands.
Government spending rises and taxes fall.
Money demand becomes zero.
q.commonError: missing that higher interest on reserves can be contractionary
q.feedback: That policy package tightens money through costlier borrowing, fewer reserves, and stronger incentives to hold reserves.

q.q: A central bank wants to close a recessionary AD gap without fiscal policy. Which chain is most accurate?
options: Buy bonds, lower rates, raise investment, shift AD right
Sell bonds, lower rates, raise investment, shift AD right
Buy bonds, raise rates, reduce investment, shift AD left
Sell bonds, raise rates, raise investment, shift AD left
q.commonError: Reversing the monetary transmission chain.
q.feedback: Expansionary monetary policy buys bonds, increases money supply, lowers rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

q.q: Which chain best explains expansionary monetary policy in the short run?
options: Fed buys bonds, money supply rises, interest rate falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
Fed sells bonds, money supply rises, interest rate falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
Fed buys bonds, money supply falls, interest rate rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
Fed raises taxes, money demand falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
q.commonError: confusing bond purchases with bond sales
q.feedback: Buying bonds increases money supply, lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

q.q: Which chain best explains contractionary monetary policy in the short run?
options: Fed sells bonds, money supply falls, interest rate rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
Fed buys bonds, money supply falls, interest rate rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
Fed sells bonds, money supply rises, interest rate falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
Fed cuts taxes, interest rates rise, AD shifts left.
q.commonError: thinking Fed bond sales expand the money supply
q.feedback: Selling bonds reduces money supply, raises interest rates, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

q.q: If the Fed reduces the money supply, which sequence is most likely?
options: Money supply shifts left, interest rates rise, and AD shifts left.
Money supply shifts right, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
Money demand shifts left, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
Money supply shifts left, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
q.commonError: reversing the interest-rate effect of lower money supply
q.feedback: A lower money supply raises interest rates, reduces investment, and shifts AD left.

q.q: If the Fed increases money supply, which sequence is most likely?
options: Money supply shifts right, interest rates fall, and AD shifts right.
Money supply shifts left, interest rates rise, and AD shifts left.
Money demand shifts right, interest rates rise, and AD shifts left.
Money supply shifts right, interest rates rise, and AD shifts left.
q.commonError: thinking more money raises interest rates in liquidity preference theory
q.feedback: A higher money supply lowers interest rates, raises investment, and shifts AD right.
