q.q: A stock market crash reduces household wealth and aggregate demand. Which Fed response best stabilizes output?
options: Increase money supply and lower interest rates.
Decrease money supply and raise interest rates.
Raise taxes and lower government spending.
Sell bonds to reduce investment.
q.commonError: choosing contractionary policy after a negative demand shock
q.feedback: A negative AD shock calls for expansionary monetary policy if the goal is stabilizing output.

q.q: An economy is overheating because aggregate demand is too high. Which Fed response best reduces inflation pressure?
options: Reduce money supply and raise interest rates.
Increase money supply and lower interest rates.
Buy bonds to raise investment.
Lower reserve requirements to shift AD right.
q.commonError: stimulating AD when AD is already excessive
q.feedback: To reduce inflation pressure from excessive AD, the Fed can tighten money and raise interest rates.

q.q: If the Fed shifts money supply right, which chain correctly reaches aggregate demand?
options: MS rises, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MS rises, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MS falls, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MD rises, r rises, investment rises, AD shifts right.
q.commonError: reversing the effect of money supply on interest rates
q.feedback: More money lowers the interest rate, raises investment, and shifts AD right.

q.q: If the Fed shifts money supply left, which chain correctly reaches aggregate demand?
options: MS falls, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MS falls, r falls, investment rises, AD shifts right.
MS rises, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
MD falls, r rises, investment falls, AD shifts left.
q.commonError: thinking less money lowers interest rates
q.feedback: Less money raises the interest rate, lowers investment, and shifts AD left.

q.q: If the Fed increases money supply but investment barely responds to the lower interest rate, what happens to the AD shift?
options: AD shifts right by less than usual because the investment channel is weak.
AD shifts right by more because investment does not matter.
AD must shift left because lower r reduces investment.
AD cannot move because money supply changed.
q.commonError: assuming the money-supply shift mechanically creates the same AD response every time
q.feedback: Monetary policy works through investment. If investment barely responds, AD shifts right less.

q.q: If the economy is in a liquidity trap, which part of the normal expansionary monetary-policy chain weakens?
options: The ability of extra money to lower r enough to boost investment
The identity that AD includes investment
The fact that money demand exists
The ability of government spending to enter AD
q.commonError: thinking liquidity trap means money demand disappears
q.feedback: In a liquidity trap, additional money may not lower interest rates enough to stimulate investment.

q.q: If money supply rises and AD shifts right, what is the correct distinction between the money-market movement and the AD-AS outcome?
options: The money market shows r falling; the AD-AS model shows higher demand for output at each price level.
The money market shows P falling; the AD-AS model shows money demand disappearing.
The money market shows taxes falling; the AD-AS model shows reserves rising.
The money market shows real output fixed by bank reserves.
q.commonError: blending the money-market graph and AD graph into one axis system
q.feedback: The money market determines the interest rate. The AD-AS model then reflects how lower rates raise spending and shift AD.

q.q: A student says, 'If the Fed buys bonds, inflation must rise immediately and real output cannot move.' Which correction is strongest?
options: In the short run, lower rates can raise AD and output before long-run price adjustment dominates.
Bond purchases only change fiscal spending, so inflation and output are unaffected.
Bond purchases lower AD because reserves rise and lending must fall.
In the long run, bond purchases permanently reduce unemployment.
q.commonError: Skipping the short-run transmission channel.
q.feedback: Open-market purchases lower interest rates and can raise AD and output in the short run.

q.q: Expansionary demand policy lowers actual unemployment from 7% to 5%, while the estimated natural rate remains 5%. Which interpretation fits the change?
options: Structural unemployment became negative
A positive cyclical unemployment gap was eliminated
The natural rate fell from 7% to 5% because demand increased
Frictional unemployment was permanently eliminated
q.commonError: Treats the natural rate as zero, fixed forever, or identical to current unemployment.
q.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

q.commonError: Assuming healthy economies should have zero unemployment.
q.q: Suppose actual unemployment is 7%, natural unemployment is 4.5%, and labor force participation is falling. What is the strongest interpretation?
options: Cyclical unemployment exists, and falling participation may hide more weakness
The labor market is definitely fully healthy
Cyclical unemployment is negative 2.5 points
Participation falling proves structural unemployment is zero
q.feedback: Actual unemployment exceeds natural unemployment by 2.5 points, and falling participation can hide additional weakness.

q.q: The pound appreciates from $1.50 to $1.65 per pound. Approximately how much does the dollar depreciate against the pound using reciprocal rates?
options: 0.1 percent
9.1 percent
10 percent
15 percent
q.commonError: Confuses a decimal rate of change with percentage units while reversing the currency quotation.
q.feedback: The reciprocal moves from 0.6667 to about 0.6061 pound per dollar, a decline of roughly 9.1 percent.

q.q: The dollar rises 20 percent in euros per dollar. Must the euro fall 20 percent in dollars per euro?
options: Yes; both reciprocal quotations rise together
No; reciprocal percentage changes have different denominators
Yes; bilateral appreciation and depreciation use the same percentage base
No; the reciprocal falls 40 percent
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Yes; bilateral appreciation and depreciation use the same percentage base” in this nominal exchange rates task.
q.feedback: If the rate moves from e to 1.2e, its reciprocal moves to 1/1.2 of its old value, a 16.7 percent decline.

q.q: A €600 appliance costs $750 at the initial rate and $720 later. What happened to the dollar against the euro?
options: The bilateral rate did not change
The dollar appreciated
The dollar depreciated
The euro appreciated
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The bilateral rate did not change” in this nominal exchange rates task.
q.feedback: The same euro price requires fewer dollars, so each dollar buys more euros.

q.q: A dollar appreciates 25 percent from 0.80 euro per dollar to 1.00. How much does the euro depreciate in reciprocal terms?
options: 25 percent
5 percent
31.25 percent
20 percent
q.commonError: Assumes reciprocal exchange-rate percentage changes have equal absolute magnitudes.
q.feedback: The reciprocal moves from $1.25 per euro to $1.00, a $0.25 decline on a $1.25 base, or 20 percent.

q.q: A €1,000 investment gains 12 percent, while the euro falls from $1.20 to $1.05. What is the investor's dollar return?
options: A loss of 2 percent
A gain of 2 percent
A gain of 12 percent
A loss of 12.5 percent
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A gain of 2 percent” in this nominal exchange rates task.
q.feedback: The initial value is $1,200. The final value is €1,120×$1.05 = $1,176, which is 2 percent lower.

q.q: Which complete chain follows a larger budget deficit in the standard model?
options: Saving falls → real interest rate rises → NCO falls → currency appreciates → NX falls
Saving falls → real interest rate falls → NCO rises → currency appreciates → NX rises
Saving rises → real interest rate rises → NCO rises → currency depreciates → NX falls
Saving falls → NCO rises → currency supply falls → currency depreciates → NX rises
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Saving falls → real interest rate falls → NCO rises → currency appreciates → NX rises” in this open economy policy transmission task.
q.feedback: The deficit lowers public and national saving, raising the real rate; lower NCO reduces FX supply, producing appreciation and lower net exports.

q.q: Political risk raises desired NCO. Why does this shift demand for loanable funds right and tend to raise the real interest rate?
options: The foreign-exchange rate becomes the price in the loanable-funds market
Government purchases replace domestic investment in the saving identity
National saving must finance both domestic investment and the larger NCO
Household consumption becomes part of NCO when political risk rises
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The foreign-exchange rate becomes the price in the loanable-funds market” in this open economy policy transmission task.
q.feedback: National saving finances I + NCO, so a larger desired NCO raises total demand for loanable funds at each real interest rate.

q.q: Political risk raises desired NCO and the equilibrium real interest rate. Which two-market outcome follows?
options: Domestic investment rises while the currency depreciates
Domestic investment falls while the domestic currency depreciates
Domestic investment rises while the currency appreciates
Domestic investment falls while the currency appreciates
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Domestic investment rises while the currency depreciates” in this open economy policy transmission task.
q.feedback: The higher loanable-funds rate crowds out domestic investment, while greater NCO shifts currency supply right and lowers the exchange rate.

q.q: A government deficit rises while foreign interest rates also rise. What is the direction of domestic NCO?
options: It falls because the domestic fiscal change receives greater weight
It rises because foreign rates determine the relevant return by themselves
It is unchanged because the NX identity offsets both rate changes
Ambiguous because the domestic-rate and foreign-rate channels oppose each other
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It falls because the domestic fiscal change receives greater weight” in this open economy policy transmission task.
q.feedback: The deficit-driven domestic rate rise tends to reduce NCO, while higher foreign returns tend to increase it.

q.q: A tariff reduces imports directly while a simultaneous budget deficit reduces national saving. What can be said about net exports?
options: Both policies raise NX through lower imports and lower saving
The tariff raises NX while the deficit changes only domestic investment
Tariff appreciation and deficit depreciation offset, leaving NX unchanged
Tariff effects are offset in equilibrium; the deficit tends to lower NX
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both policies raise NX through lower imports and lower saving” in this open economy policy transmission task.
q.feedback: Trade policy is offset by appreciation when NCO is fixed; the deficit lowers NCO and therefore lowers the equilibrium NX balance.

q.q: Monetary tightening raises the domestic interest rate, while political risk simultaneously rises. What can be concluded about the currency?
options: It is unchanged because monetary policy affects the nominal rate while risk affects the real rate
Its direction is ambiguous because lower NCO from returns opposes higher NCO from risk
It appreciates because the policy-rate channel is transmitted before portfolios rebalance
It depreciates because political risk shifts currency demand rather than supply
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It is unchanged because monetary policy affects the nominal rate while risk affects the real rate” in this open economy policy transmission task.
q.feedback: Higher returns tend to reduce currency supply and appreciate the currency; higher risk tends to raise supply and depreciate it.

q.q: After capital flight, the real interest rate rises and domestic investment falls. Why can NCO still be higher?
options: The higher interest rate moves NCO outward along its unchanged relationship
Domestic investment and NCO move together because both use national saving
Capital flight reclassifies foreign assets as domestic investment
The outward shift in desired foreign assets exceeds the rate-induced movement back toward domestic assets
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The higher interest rate moves NCO outward along its unchanged relationship” in this open economy policy transmission task.
q.feedback: The risk shock shifts the NCO relationship outward; the higher rate partly offsets but need not reverse that shift.

q.q: The government deficit widens and private saving rises by the same amount. What happens through the national-saving channel?
options: National saving falls by twice the deficit change, strengthening the usual chain
NCO falls because public saving receives more weight than private saving
The currency appreciates because the deficit shifts FX supply directly
National saving is unchanged, so the standard deficit chain need not begin
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving falls by twice the deficit change, strengthening the usual chain” in this open economy policy transmission task.
q.feedback: The offsetting private-saving increase leaves total national saving unchanged, removing the stated first link.

q.q: Capital flight raises NCO and the real interest rate. Which outcomes follow in the two markets?
options: More currency demand, appreciation, and less investment
Less currency demand, depreciation, and more investment
More currency supply, depreciation, and less domestic investment
Less currency supply, appreciation, and more investment
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “More currency demand, appreciation, and less investment” in this open economy policy transmission task.
q.feedback: Higher NCO shifts FX supply right, while the higher loanable-funds rate crowds out some domestic investment.

q.q: Which event shifts both SRAS left and SRPC up-right?
options: Oil price surge
Tax cut
Open-market purchase
Consumer confidence boom
q.commonError: Confusing supply shocks with AD shocks.
q.feedback: An oil price surge raises production costs and worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

q.q: A central bank unexpectedly expands AD. Later, workers build the higher inflation into wage demands. Which sequence is most accurate?
options: Move along SRPC, then SRPC shifts up
SRPC shifts down, then move along LRPC
LRPC shifts left, then AD falls
Move along LRAS, then M1 falls
q.commonError: Confusing immediate inflation surprise with later expectation adjustment.
q.feedback: Unexpected AD expansion first moves along the SRPC; later expected inflation rises and shifts SRPC upward.

q.q: A policymaker says, 'Inflation is high, so unemployment must be low.' What is the best correction?
options: That only fits demand pressure; supply shocks can raise inflation and unemployment together.
That is always true because the Phillips curve never shifts.
That is false only when M1 is larger than M2.
That is true in the long run because LRPC slopes downward.
q.commonError: Treating the Phillips curve as fixed under every shock.
q.feedback: The short-run tradeoff can worsen when SRPC shifts up, so inflation and unemployment can rise together.

q.q: Actual inflation is 5% while wage setters expected 3%, temporarily pushing unemployment below natural. What erodes that effect?
options: The price level returns to its initial value automatically
Forecasts adjust upward, shifting the SRPC until unemployment returns toward natural
The LRPC shifts left because actual inflation is above expected
Forecasts adjust downward, moving unemployment farther below natural
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
q.feedback: As expected inflation adapts, the temporary unemployment effect fades and the SRPC shifts.

q.q: A supply shock raises inflation without a demand boom. Why might a simple expectations-only diagnosis be incomplete?
options: Expected inflation is the only possible SRPC shifter in the introductory model
Every inflation increase is movement along a fixed SRPC regardless of its cause
Supply shocks shift only the vertical LRPC while leaving SRPC unchanged
The shock can shift the SRPC even before expectations adapt
q.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
q.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

q.q: An adverse supply shock raises actual inflation, then wage setters incorporate it into next year’s contracts. What are the two stages?
options: An initial SRPC shift followed by reinforcement through higher expected inflation
Two movements along one fixed SRPC with no change in the inflation-unemployment relation
An LRPC shift followed by lower expected inflation when contracts renew
A demand contraction followed by an SRPC shift downward at each unemployment rate
q.commonError: Assumes a surprise to actual inflation remains a surprise indefinitely.
q.feedback: The supply shock first shifts SRPC upward even with expectations unchanged. Incorporating the higher observed inflation into contracts adds an expectations-driven upward shift. This reinforces inflation pressure rather than describing the disappearance of a demand-created unemployment gain.

q.q: A subsidy is predicted to raise enrollment and is therefore recommended. Which split is correct?
options: Both parts are positive because enrollment can be measured
Both parts are normative because a subsidy is a policy
The forecast is positive; the recommendation is normative
The forecast is normative; the recommendation is positive.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: “The policy benefits most residents, so it is just.” Where is the normative step?
options: The claim that most residents benefit
The number of residents affected by the policy
The measured size of the benefits.
Calling the distribution just
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: What could test the claim that a road fee reduces congestion?
options: Traffic counts around comparable fee changes
A survey asking whether drivers think the fee is fair
A city council vote on the fee
A statement from officials that the fee will work.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: When can “the project has positive net benefits” be positive?
options: Always, because net benefits are measured in dollars
When inputs and the net-benefit rule are empirically checkable
Never, because the word benefits is inherently normative
Only when everyone agrees the project is desirable.
q.commonError: Treating positive as good, true, or politically neutral.
q.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

q.q: “The only acceptable policy is universal access.” Why is this normative?
options: Universal access can be measured
The statement refers to a policy outcome
It embeds a value standard despite objective wording
The sentence does not include a numerical prediction.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A rule lowers costs but is called morally wrong. What can evidence settle?
options: Both the cost effect and whether the rule is morally wrong
Only whether the rule is morally wrong
Neither claim, because the rule is a policy.
The cost effect, but not the moral conclusion by itself
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: A report defines success only as maximum total surplus. What choice is normative?
options: Calculating total surplus from observed prices and quantities
Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
Measuring how total surplus changes after the policy
Estimating the policy’s effect on output.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A report predicts gains and calls them worth unequal losses. What is normative?
options: The judgment that gains justify the losses
The prediction that the policy creates gains
The estimated size of the gains
The measured distribution of gains and losses.
q.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
q.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

q.q: What best tests “a fee reduces congestion”?
options: A survey asking whether residents support the fee
Traffic counts before and after comparable changes
A council vote to adopt the fee
A statement from officials that congestion will fall.
q.commonError: Assuming objective wording alone makes a claim positive.
q.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

q.q: Why is “Policy A is responsible” not automatically positive?
options: The statement mentions a policy
The word responsible refers to a measurable outcome
Responsible may hide an unstated value standard
Any sentence about policy performance is positive.
q.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
q.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

q.q: A new technology improves only the production of Good X, not Good Y. What happens to the PPF?
options: It shifts inward equally for both goods
It creates a shortage of Good Y
It becomes a price ceiling
It rotates outward on the Good X axis
q.commonError: thinks_all_growth_shifts_both_axes_equally
q.feedback: Technology that helps only one good expands production possibilities for that good, rotating the PPF outward on that axis.

q.q: A country invests more in capital goods today, sacrificing consumer goods. In a PPF framework, what is the likely long-run implication?
options: More future growth because capital accumulation can expand productive capacity
No future effect because PPF choices never matter
Immediate elimination of scarcity because future productive capacity will be larger.
A binding price floor in the capital market
q.commonError: misses_current_consumption_future_growth_tradeoff
q.feedback: Choosing more capital goods today can increase future productive capacity and shift the PPF outward later.

q.q: A new technology improves only production of medical devices, not food. Which PPF interpretation is best?
options: The entire frontier must shift inward
The economy moves inside the PPF
The frontier rotates outward on the medical-device axis
The law of demand no longer applies
q.commonError: thinks_all_technology_shifts_both_goods_equally
q.feedback: Technology that improves only one good expands capacity for that good, rotating the PPF outward along that axis.

q.q: A disaster destroys equipment used only to produce electric power, while agricultural capacity is unchanged. What happens to the PPF?
options: It shifts outward equally for both goods.
It pivots inward toward the agricultural axis only.
Only the electric-power intercept moves inward.
It remains fixed because the economy can move along the frontier.
q.commonError: Treating a sector-specific loss as an equal inward shift or a movement along the same frontier.
q.feedback: Losing capacity in one sector reduces the maximum output of that good and rotates the frontier inward on that axis.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: Output rises from 10,000 units to 12,000 units while labor rises from 100 workers to 150 workers. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 100 units per worker to 80 units per worker
It rises from 100 units per worker to 120 units per worker
It stays at 100 units per worker
It cannot be calculated
q.feedback: Initial productivity is 100; new productivity is 12000/150 = 80, so productivity falls.

q.q: Output per worker rises, but output per labor hour is unchanged. Which explanation is consistent with both facts?
options: Total output must have fallen
The labor force must have shrunk to zero
Average hours worked per worker increased
Every worker became more productive per hour
q.commonError: Confuses total output with output per unit of labor.
q.feedback: If output per worker rises while output per hour is unchanged, each worker must be working more hours on average.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: Output rises from 50,000 to 60,000 while labor hours rise from 10,000 to 12,500. What happens to productivity?
options: It falls from 5 to 4.8 units per hour
It rises from 5 to 6 units per hour
It stays at 5 units per hour
It rises from 4.8 to 5 units per hour
q.feedback: Initial productivity = 50,000/10,000 = 5. New productivity = 60,000/12,500 = 4.8.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: A country raises output by increasing labor force participation, but output per worker falls. What is the most precise conclusion?
options: Total production rose, but productivity declined
Living standards must have doubled
Productivity rose because employment rose
Real GDP cannot rise when productivity falls
q.feedback: More workers can raise total output even while output per worker falls.

q.commonError: Confusing total output with output per unit of labor.
q.q: Workers produce 500 units in 1,000 hours before training and 650 units in 1,000 hours after training. What happened?
options: Productivity rose from 0.5 to 0.65 units per hour
Productivity fell from 2 to 1.54 units per hour
Productivity stayed constant
Output rose but productivity cannot change
q.feedback: Productivity is output per hour: 500/1000 = 0.5 and 650/1000 = 0.65.

q.q: Which statement best combines quantity theory and monetary neutrality?
options: Money growth mainly affects prices in the long run, while real output depends on real factors.
Money growth permanently raises real output and leaves prices unchanged.
Money growth lowers all nominal variables and raises real wages.
Money growth has no effect on nominal or real variables.
q.commonError: thinking long-run money growth is mainly a real-output policy
q.feedback: In the long run, money growth mainly shows up in nominal variables like prices, while real output depends on real resources and productivity.

q.q: The money supply rises once by 10 percent while velocity and real output remain fixed. What does the quantity theory predict?
options: The inflation rate remains 10 percent every year even if money stops growing.
Real output rises permanently by 10 percent with no price change.
The price level rises once; continued inflation needs continued money growth.
Velocity must fall by 10 percent to preserve the equation.
q.commonError: Confusing a one-time increase in the price level with a permanently higher inflation rate.
q.feedback: With velocity and real output fixed, a one-time money increase produces a one-time proportional price-level increase.

q.q: Money growth rises, velocity falls, and output rises. Which statement is safest?
options: Inflation depends on all three changes
Inflation must equal money growth
Inflation must be zero
Inflation must exceed output growth
q.commonError: Using money growth alone when V and Y change.
q.feedback: The quantity equation connects money, velocity, prices, and output, so inflation depends on changes in all of them.

q.q: If money demand shifts right while money supply is unchanged in the value-of-money model, what is the likely new equilibrium?
options: Higher value of money and lower price level
Lower value of money and higher price level
Higher money supply and higher price level
Lower money demand and lower value of money
q.commonError: treating all rightward shifts as inflationary regardless of axis meaning
q.feedback: With fixed money supply, higher money demand pushes up the value of money, which means the price level falls.

q.q: Starting at the original equilibrium, the Fed increases money supply. Which complete chain is correct?
options: MS shifts right, excess money appears at the old price level, spending rises, P rises, and the value of money falls.
MS shifts left, excess money appears, spending rises, P falls, and the value of money rises.
MD shifts right, money supply stays fixed, P falls, and value of money rises.
MS shifts right, spending falls, P falls, and the value of money rises.
q.commonError: getting the direction of value of money backward
q.feedback: A monetary injection shifts MS right. At the old price level there is excess money, which fuels spending, raises P, and lowers the value of money.

q.q: At the old equilibrium value of money after MS shifts right, what disequilibrium exists and what removes it?
options: Excess supply of money; people spend or lend excess balances until prices rise.
Excess demand for money; people sell goods until prices fall.
Excess supply of goods; people hoard money until the price level falls.
No disequilibrium; the value of money changes without behavior.
q.commonError: missing why prices rise after excess money appears
q.feedback: At the old price level, the higher money supply creates excess money balances. People spend or lend them, pushing prices up.

q.q: A student argues that equal inflation rates guarantee an unchanged real exchange rate. What is missing?
options: Domestic prices cannot be measured
PPP rules out equal inflation
The foreign price level must equal one
The nominal exchange rate may change
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The foreign price level must equal one” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
q.feedback: Equal inflation stabilizes the price-level ratio, but nominal exchange-rate movements can still change eP/P*.

q.q: A nominal appreciation occurs while the real exchange rate depreciates. Which combination can produce both?
options: Domestic and foreign inflation are equal
The nominal rate rises and domestic inflation also rises faster
Foreign inflation exceeds domestic inflation by more than the nominal appreciation
Domestic inflation exceeds foreign inflation by the same amount
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The nominal rate rises and domestic inflation also rises faster” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
q.feedback: A sufficiently large fall in P/P* can outweigh the rise in e, causing eP/P* to decline.

q.q: Why can a tariff create a persistent price wedge without disproving the logic behind PPP?
options: The tariff converts real prices into nominal prices
PPP excludes traded goods from comparison
A tariff fixes the nominal exchange rate
The tariff is a trade cost that limits arbitrage
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “The tariff converts real prices into nominal prices” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
q.feedback: PPP's equalization force is weakened by costs and barriers that prevent price differences from being profitably arbitraged.

q.q: A real appreciation makes domestic goods relatively more expensive. How does this connect to net exports?
options: Exports tend to rise because domestic goods cost more
Imports tend to fall because foreign goods become relatively cheaper
Exports tend to fall and imports tend to rise, reducing NX
Exports and imports both rise by equal amounts
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Exports tend to rise because domestic goods cost more” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
q.feedback: A higher real exchange rate shifts spending toward foreign goods, lowering exports minus imports.

q.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
q.q: Nominal GDP rises from $20T to $22T while real GDP rises from $18T to $18.9T. What is the best interpretation?
options: Both prices and real output likely rose
Only real output rose
Only prices rose
Neither prices nor output changed
q.feedback: Real GDP rose 5%, while nominal GDP rose 10%, so both output and prices likely increased.

q.q: Nominal GDP falls 2 percent while the GDP deflator falls 5 percent. What is the best approximate conclusion?
options: Real GDP falls about 7 percent.
Real GDP rises about 3 percent.
Real GDP falls about 3 percent.
Real GDP is unchanged.
q.commonError: Adding nominal and price changes instead of separating them.
q.feedback: Approximate real GDP growth equals nominal GDP growth minus inflation in the deflator: −2% − (−5%) = about 3%.

q.commonError: Forgetting to subtract inflation from the nominal interest rate.
q.q: Nominal interest is 12%, actual inflation is 8%, and expected inflation was 5%. What are actual and expected real interest rates?
options: Actual 4%; expected 7%
Actual 7%; expected 4%
Actual 20%; expected 17%
Actual -4%; expected -7%
q.feedback: Actual real = 12 - 8 = 4. Expected real = 12 - 5 = 7.

q.q: A fixed-rate borrower and lender expected 2% inflation, but actual inflation is 8%. The nominal rate is 7%. What happened?
options: The real rate fell from about 5% to about −1%, helping the borrower
The real rate rose from 5% to 15%, helping the lender
Both parties still received the expected five-percent real outcome because the nominal loan rate remained fixed
The nominal rate automatically adjusted to 13%
q.commonError: Misses how unexpected inflation changes the real burden of a fixed nominal loan.
q.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real repayment burden and shifts purchasing power from lender to borrower.

q.q: A student says disinflation has no cost if the Fed announces it. What is the correction?
options: Credibility can lower the cost, not guarantee zero cost
Announcements always raise inflation first
The sacrifice ratio ignores expectations
Unemployment must fall during disinflation
q.commonError: Overstating credibility effects.
q.feedback: Credibility can reduce the sacrifice ratio, but it does not automatically make disinflation costless.

q.q: The Fed announces disinflation, but workers doubt it and expected inflation stays high. What happens to the sacrifice ratio?
options: It is likely higher
It is automatically zero
It becomes the MPC
It shifts LRAS right
q.commonError: Assuming announcements alone make policy credible.
q.feedback: If expected inflation does not fall quickly, reducing actual inflation tends to require more output loss.

q.q: A disinflation plan is credible, wage contracts adjust quickly, and expected inflation falls fast. Which path is most likely?
options: Smaller unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
Larger unemployment increase for the same inflation reduction
No change in expected inflation despite credibility
Permanent unemployment below natural
q.commonError: Ignoring expectations in sacrifice-ratio logic.
q.feedback: Credibility and fast expectation adjustment reduce the output and unemployment cost of lowering inflation.

q.q: A disinflation plan lacks credibility, wage contracts are slow, and expected inflation remains high. Which path is most likely?
options: Larger output loss for the same inflation reduction
Smaller output loss for the same inflation reduction
Immediate movement to lower unemployment
LRPC becomes downward sloping
q.commonError: Assuming disinflation costs vanish without credibility.
q.feedback: If expected inflation stays high, lowering actual inflation usually requires a larger output loss.

q.q: Output rises by $100, consumption rises by $70, and government purchases rise by $10. What happens to national saving and loanable-funds supply?
options: National saving rises by $20, so loanable-funds supply shifts right
National saving falls by $20, so loanable-funds supply shifts left
National saving rises by $180, so investment demand shifts right
National saving is unchanged because output and spending all increased
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving falls by $20, so loanable-funds supply shifts left” in this saving and investment identities task.
q.feedback: Using S = Y − C − G, the change is +100 − 70 − 10 = +$20. Higher national saving shifts the loanable-funds supply curve right.

q.q: Net taxes are $320 and government purchases are $280. Private saving then falls by $20 while fiscal quantities remain fixed. What follows?
options: Public saving falls to $20, but national saving remains unchanged
Public saving remains $40, while national saving rises $20 and supply shifts right
Public saving rises to $60, shifting investment demand rather than loanable-funds supply
Public saving stays $40; national saving falls $20
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Public saving falls to $20, but national saving remains unchanged” in this saving and investment identities task.
q.feedback: Public saving remains T − G = $40 because fiscal quantities do not change. The $20 decline in private saving therefore lowers national saving and shifts supply left.

q.q: In a closed economy, Y=$700, C=$420, net taxes T=$140, and G=$210. Which saving decomposition reconciles the identity?
options: Private saving $140, public saving +$70, national saving $210
Private saving $70, public saving $140, national saving $210
Private saving $140, public saving −$70, national saving and investment $70
Private saving $280, public saving −$70, national saving $210
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Private saving $140, public saving +$70, national saving $210” in this saving and investment identities task.
q.feedback: Private saving=Y−T−C=140; public=T−G=−70; national=Y−C−G=70. In the stated closed-economy identity, I=S=70.

q.q: Private saving rises by $25 billion while public saving falls by $40 billion. What happens in the loanable-funds market, all else equal?
options: National saving rises by $65 billion, shifting supply right and lowering the real rate
National saving rises by $15 billion, shifting investment demand right and raising the real rate
National saving is unchanged because private and public saving always offset one another
National saving falls by $15 billion, shifting supply left and raising the equilibrium real rate
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving rises by $65 billion, shifting supply right and lowering the real rate” in this saving and investment identities task.
q.feedback: The two components change national saving by +25 − 40 = −$15 billion. Lower national saving shifts loanable-funds supply left, raising the real rate and reducing equilibrium investment.

q.q: If net taxes rise by $20 while income, consumption, and government purchases stay fixed, what happens to national saving?
options: It rises by $20
It remains unchanged
It falls by $20
It becomes equal to net taxes
q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “It rises by $20” in this saving and investment identities task.
q.feedback: Private saving falls by $20 while public saving rises by $20, so their sum and Y − C − G are unchanged.

q.q: A policy increases total output but leaves the lowest-income group worse off. Which judgment is most accurate?
options: It may improve total output while worsening the distribution of gains
It must improve both efficiency and equality because output increased
It eliminates scarcity because the economy can now produce more output
It cannot improve efficiency because at least one affected group loses
q.commonError: Assuming efficiency and equality are the same criterion.
q.feedback: Efficiency and distribution are separate dimensions, so they can move in opposite directions.

q.q: A reform raises average income and narrows the income gap but requires more administrative resources. Which statement is warranted?
options: Efficiency and equality cannot improve at the same time
Publicly funded administrative resources are not scarce
The reform may improve both efficiency and equality while still using scarce resources.
There is no tradeoff because average income and equality both improve.
q.commonError: Treating tradeoffs as proof that every objective must worsen.
q.feedback: Some policies can improve multiple outcomes, but resource use and implementation constraints still matter.

q.q: A policy expands total production, reduces pollution, and requires a small tax increase. Which statement is most defensible?
options: Several goals may improve, while taxes and inputs still have alternative uses
Several benefits mean the policy uses no scarce resources or public funds
Scarcity matters only when total production falls after the policy change
Any tax increase proves the policy reduces both efficiency and equality
q.commonError: Using a single outcome to judge a multi-dimensional policy.
q.feedback: A complete tradeoff analysis includes gains, resource use, financing, and distribution.

q.q: A government can increase disaster preparedness by diverting engineers from current infrastructure repairs. The preparedness program is highly valuable. What still follows?
options: Public projects do not compete for scarce inputs
Its value does not remove the tradeoff created by limited engineering capacity.
Only money, not skilled labor, can be scarce
A highly valuable program has no resource cost.
q.commonError: Treating high value as proof of no sacrifice.
q.feedback: Even high-value projects require scarce labor, time, and materials that could serve other purposes.

q.q: An allocation rule maximizes total output but concentrates nearly all gains among a small group. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The rule may be efficient by one criterion while raising serious equality concerns.
Scarcity prevents economists from discussing how gains are distributed
High total output automatically makes the allocation equal
Any unequal allocation must reduce total output.
q.commonError: Using efficiency as a complete moral judgment.
q.feedback: Efficiency and equality are distinct criteria and should be evaluated separately.

q.q: An evacuation plan dedicates the only outbound bridge to buses carrying people without cars, delaying private vehicles. Which statement is most complete?
options: The rule reallocates scarce road capacity and changes who bears delay
Prioritizing vulnerable residents creates additional bridge capacity
A fairness goal makes the delay imposed on other users economically irrelevant
The bridge is not scarce because evacuees are not charged a toll
q.commonError: Treating a fairness rationale as elimination of the underlying capacity cost.
q.feedback: The priority rule affects distribution, but the bridge capacity remains fixed.

q.q: A policy improves equity but reduces total surplus. Which answer best frames the issue?
options: It presents an efficiency-equity tradeoff requiring both criteria
It proves the policy is desirable because equity necessarily dominates
It proves the policy is undesirable because total surplus necessarily dominates
It removes scarcity because one distributional goal improves
q.commonError: treats_tradeoff_as_automatic_policy_answer
q.feedback: Policies often involve tradeoffs. A reduction in efficiency may or may not be justified by equity goals.

q.q: A coastal city can use a limited parcel for flood protection, affordable housing, or commercial development. Which analysis best respects scarcity?
options: Compare feasible parcel uses, incremental benefits and displaced uses, making the distribution of gains and losses explicit.
Rank uses by expected cash revenue, counting public benefits only when the city can charge users for them.
Rank uses by the number of beneficiaries, treating benefit size and displaced alternatives as secondary tie-breakers.
Divide the parcel equally among uses, treating equal area shares as sufficient evidence of equal benefit and efficiency.
q.commonError: Listing benefits without confronting mutually exclusive uses.
q.feedback: A scarce parcel requires a feasible comparison of valued uses, including nonmarket benefits and distribution. Cash revenue, beneficiary counts or equal acreage alone can miss opportunity costs and competing criteria.

q.q: A wage floor raises pay for workers who keep jobs but reduces entry-level openings. Which economic idea best frames the policy debate?
options: An efficiency-equity tradeoff
A movement along the PPF with no opportunity cost
A nonbinding ceiling
A fixed CPI basket
q.commonError: analyzes_only_winners_or_only_losers
q.feedback: The policy can improve outcomes for some workers while reducing efficiency or job access for others.

q.q: A breakthrough makes desalination much cheaper, but coastal land, energy, pipelines, and environmental capacity remain limited. Which statement is best?
options: Cheaper desalination reduces water opportunity cost to zero, leaving land and energy limits relevant only for other industries.
Cheaper desalination relaxes one constraint, but land, energy and delivery limits can become the binding sources of tradeoffs.
Cheaper desalination makes physical water abundant, so any remaining scarcity must be explained entirely by monopoly pricing.
Cheaper desalination expands output proportionally at every stage, so pipelines and environmental limits become less binding automatically.
q.commonError: Assuming one technological improvement removes all constraints.
q.feedback: A productivity improvement changes which resource limits output. Complementary land, energy, networks and environmental capacity remain scarce and need not expand with desalination technology.

q.q: An aid aircraft can carry water filters, antibiotics, or shelter materials after a cyclone. Which decision process best applies scarcity reasoning?
options: Compare marginal relief benefits per constrained cargo unit and identify the urgent needs displaced by each feasible load.
Load the items serving the largest headcount, treating differences in treatment benefit and cargo weight as secondary.
Divide weight equally across the three supplies, treating equal shares as proof of the greatest total relief benefit.
Load the highest-priced supplies first, treating purchase prices as complete measures of local marginal relief value.
q.commonError: Using a single rule while ignoring cargo capacity and the supplies displaced.
q.feedback: Scarce payload requires comparing benefits against space or weight and the supplies forgone. Headcounts, equal weights and purchase prices alone do not identify the best load.

q.q: A city allocates scarce shelter beds by medical vulnerability instead of willingness to pay. What changes?
options: The allocation rule changes, while the limited number of beds does not
The vulnerability rule immediately creates enough beds for every applicant
The beds stop being scarce because recipients do not bid a money price
The rule makes efficiency and equality identical measures of the outcome
q.commonError: Assuming rationing rules remove the constraint.
q.feedback: The rule determines recipients but does not create more beds.

q.q: A technology raises output and reduces input use, yet firms still choose among projects. Why?
options: Remaining capital, skilled labor, time, and wants still create choices
Higher productivity guarantees that every available project can be funded
Only government agencies continue to face tradeoffs after technology improves
Productivity growth changes scarcity into a temporary market shortage
q.commonError: Assuming productivity growth eliminates choice.
q.feedback: Productivity relaxes constraints but does not remove all competing uses.

q.q: Which evaluation is most complete for a policy that increases output but harms a vulnerable group?
options: Reject the policy solely because one group loses
Assume there is no tradeoff because output rises
Evaluate only the change in total output.
Assess both the total gains and the distribution of gains and losses.
q.commonError: Using only one criterion in a multi-dimensional judgment.
q.feedback: Economic evaluation should separate efficiency from distributional effects.

q.q: Oil prices rise sharply, but firms also adopt a productivity-enhancing technology. What can be concluded about SRAS?
options: Oil costs push SRAS left and productivity pushes it right; magnitudes determine the net shift
Oil costs push SRAS right and productivity pushes it right; both raise short-run supply
Oil costs push SRAS left and productivity pushes it left; both lower short-run supply
Oil costs push SRAS left and productivity pushes it right; opposing signs establish an unchanged curve
q.commonError: Allowing one supply shifter to dominate without magnitude information.
q.feedback: Higher oil costs push SRAS left, while higher productivity pushes it right.

q.q: A government permanently improves transportation infrastructure but finances it with a temporary business-energy surcharge. Which supply effects are possible?
options: Only AD can change.
LRAS may shift right while SRAS shifts left temporarily.
Both LRAS and SRAS must shift left permanently.
LRAS must remain fixed because taxes are involved.
q.commonError: Treating all policy effects as demand-side or same-direction.
q.feedback: Infrastructure can raise capacity while the temporary surcharge raises current production costs.

q.q: A severe storm destroys capital, while emergency deregulation lowers current compliance costs. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Capital destruction reduces LRAS; cost relief shifts only AD, so the SRAS direction is certainly left
Capital destruction reduces LRAS; its adverse SRAS effect competes with lower compliance costs, leaving net SRAS uncertain
Capital destruction reduces LRAS; lower compliance costs also reduce SRAS, so both short-run forces shift supply left
Lower compliance costs raise LRAS; capital destruction affects only SRAS, so long-run capacity rises
q.commonError: Assuming all supply forces have the same horizon and direction.
q.feedback: Capital destruction lowers capacity; lower compliance cost pushes SRAS right, while storm disruption may push it left.

q.q: Expected inflation rises, productivity improves, and oil prices fall. What can be concluded about SRAS?
options: Left: expected inflation and productivity shift SRAS left, oil shifts it right
Right: all three changes shift the SRAS curve right
Unchanged: the opposing SRAS shifts necessarily cancel each other
Ambiguous: expectations shift SRAS left, productivity and oil shift it right
q.commonError: Ignoring offsetting supply shifters.
q.feedback: Multiple cost and productivity forces push SRAS in opposite directions.

q.q: Productivity rises permanently, expected prices rise, and oil prices fall. What is the most accurate result?
options: Higher expected prices lower LRAS; productivity and cheaper oil raise SRAS, so the curves move in opposite directions
Productivity leaves LRAS fixed; expected prices and cheaper oil offset in SRAS, so both curves remain unchanged
Productivity raises LRAS; higher expected prices oppose productivity and cheaper oil in SRAS, so its net direction is uncertain
Productivity raises LRAS; expected prices and cheaper oil reinforce productivity in SRAS, so both curves shift right
q.commonError: Forcing offsetting SRAS shifters into one predetermined direction.
q.feedback: Productivity raises capacity; expected prices and oil prices push SRAS in opposite directions.

q.q: A policymaker claims higher inflation can permanently hold unemployment below natural. What is the flaw?
options: Expected inflation adjusts over time
Money demand is always zero
LRAS shifts right automatically
M1 excludes currency
q.commonError: Believing in a permanent Phillips curve menu.
q.feedback: Once expected inflation adjusts, unemployment returns to the natural rate.

q.q: Which answer best separates short-run and long-run Phillips curve logic?
options: Policy can move unemployment temporarily, but expectations restore the natural rate
Policy cannot affect unemployment even briefly, because money is neutral in every period
Policy permanently lowers unemployment whenever inflation rises above zero
Policy shifts LRPC whenever actual inflation changes
q.commonError: Confusing short-run effects with long-run neutrality.
q.feedback: Demand policy can move unemployment in the short run, but expectations adjust and unemployment returns to natural.

q.q: An adverse supply shock raises inflation while output falls. How should the AD-AS result transfer to the Phillips model?
options: Higher inflation and unemployment indicate an upward SRPC shift
Higher inflation and lower unemployment indicate movement along SRPC
Lower inflation and unemployment indicate a downward SRPC shift
Unchanged inflation with lower unemployment indicates an LRPC shift
q.commonError: Calls a supply or expectations shock a movement along one unchanged SRPC.
q.feedback: A changed inflation-unemployment relationship shifts the SRPC; it is not movement along the same curve.

q.q: A policymaker cites the downward-sloping SRPC as proof that permanently higher inflation will secure permanently lower unemployment. What is the decisive flaw?
options: The SRPC actually slopes upward for every demand change
Inflation cannot respond to aggregate demand in the short run
The natural rate is always zero after an expansion
Expected inflation adjusts, so the short-run unemployment gain is not permanent
q.commonError: Treats the short-run association as a permanent menu of policy choices.
q.feedback: On a given SRPC, lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation only in the short run.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A country has abundant natural resources but weak education, poor infrastructure, and unstable property rights. What is the best growth interpretation?
options: Resources need skills, capital, technology, and institutions
Natural resources guarantee high living standards
Education is irrelevant if resources are abundant
GDP must equal natural resource value
q.feedback: Natural resources help, but productivity also depends on skills, capital, technology, and institutions.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A country discovers oil but has weak courts, low education, and poor infrastructure. Why might productivity remain low?
options: Resources alone do not guarantee high productivity
Oil is not a natural resource
Education matters only in service economies
Infrastructure lowers capital per worker
q.feedback: Natural resources can help, but productivity depends on several complementary factors.

q.commonError: Confusing tools and equipment with worker skills.
q.q: A low-capital economy gets basic tools and output jumps sharply. Later, additional tools add smaller gains. Which pattern is this?
options: Catch-up effect followed by diminishing returns
CPI substitution bias followed by inflation
Frictional unemployment followed by cyclical unemployment
Imports followed by exports
q.feedback: Capital is highly productive when scarce, but additional capital eventually yields smaller gains.

q.q: Congress cuts government spending to reduce the deficit. If the Fed wants to stabilize output, what should it do?
options: Increase money supply to lower interest rates and support AD.
Decrease money supply to raise interest rates and reduce AD further.
Raise taxes to lower consumption further.
Do nothing because fiscal policy cannot affect AD.
q.commonError: doubling down on contraction after AD falls
q.feedback: A spending cut shifts AD left. Expansionary monetary policy can partly offset that.

q.q: A supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why is the policy response harder than for a pure demand shock?
options: Stimulating AD may raise output somewhat but can worsen inflation.
Stimulating AD always lowers prices and raises output with no tradeoff.
Contractionary policy always raises output.
Supply shocks only affect money demand.
q.commonError: treating every downturn like a demand shock
q.feedback: A supply shock creates a tradeoff: boosting aggregate demand may support output but can add inflation pressure.

q.q: A negative AD shock reduces output and the price level. Which policy response best targets the shock without relying on supply-side repair?
options: Expansionary monetary or fiscal policy to shift AD right
Contractionary policy to shift AD left
Higher taxes and lower government spending
A policy that reduces investment spending
q.commonError: using contractionary policy against weak demand
q.feedback: A negative AD shock calls for policies that shift AD right if the goal is stabilizing output.

q.q: An economy is above potential output because AD is too high. Which response best reduces the boom without increasing AD further?
options: Contractionary monetary policy or contractionary fiscal policy
Expansionary monetary policy and tax cuts
Higher government spending and lower interest rates
Bond purchases and larger deficits
q.commonError: stimulating an economy that is already overheating
q.feedback: When AD is too high, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

q.q: A recessionary demand shock hits, but the Fed is at the zero lower bound. Which option best describes the policy problem?
options: AD needs support, but rate cuts have limited room
AD is too high, and rate cuts work too strongly
SRAS needs support, but wages rise instantly
LRPC must shift, but M2 is too small
q.commonError: Ignoring why zero rates weaken monetary stimulus.
q.feedback: When rates are near zero, traditional monetary policy may struggle to shift AD right enough.

q.q: Fiscal stimulus raises AD, but the central bank offsets it with tighter money. Which final outcome is most plausible?
options: AD rises less than fiscal policy alone suggests
AD rises more than fiscal policy alone suggests
SRAS shifts right because interest rates rise
LRPC shifts left because taxes fall
q.commonError: Ignoring policy interactions.
q.feedback: Tighter monetary policy can offset fiscal stimulus by raising interest rates and weakening AD.

q.q: Congress cuts spending during a recession while the Fed also sells bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD left or reduce support for AD, worsening the demand problem.
Both policies shift AD right, stabilizing output.
Fiscal policy shifts AD right while monetary policy shifts AD right.
Neither policy affects AD.
q.commonError: missing that Fed bond sales are contractionary
q.feedback: Cutting spending reduces AD, and Fed bond sales raise rates and reduce investment. That is contraction on top of contraction.

q.q: Congress raises spending during an inflationary boom while the Fed buys bonds. What is the combined AD effect?
options: Both policies shift AD right, risking more inflation pressure.
Both policies shift AD left, reducing inflation pressure.
Fiscal policy shifts AD left while monetary policy shifts AD left.
Neither affects AD because output is already high.
q.commonError: thinking expansionary policy is always appropriate
q.feedback: Spending increases and bond purchases both shift AD right. During an inflationary boom, that pours gasoline on the fire.

q.q: A negative supply shock reduces output and raises prices. Why can expansionary AD policy be a blunt tool here?
options: It may raise output somewhat but can worsen the price-level increase.
It directly restores lost productive capacity with no inflation risk.
It shifts SRAS right automatically.
It lowers prices and lowers output at the same time.
q.commonError: treating supply shocks like pure demand shocks
q.feedback: AD stimulus can support spending, but it does not fix the supply loss and may worsen inflation.

q.q: An adverse supply shock reduces output by 30 and raises inflation. Which policy comparison recognizes the constraint facing demand management?
options: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
Support: output and inflation fall; restraint: output and inflation rise.
Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
Support: potential output rises; restraint: potential output falls by reversing the disruption.
q.commonError: Incorrect inference: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
q.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-output tradeoff. Demand management changes the position on that tradeoff; it does not directly repair the supply cause.

q.q: An adverse supply shock reduces output by 70 and raises inflation. Which policy comparison recognizes the constraint facing demand management?
options: Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
Support: output and inflation fall; restraint: output and inflation rise.
Support: potential output rises; restraint: potential output falls by reversing the disruption.
q.commonError: Incorrect inference: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
q.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-output tradeoff. Demand management changes the position on that tradeoff; it does not directly repair the supply cause.

q.q: A seller-side tax shifts the supply curve upward. Which statement best explains why buyers still pay part of the tax?
options: Elasticities determine how the tax is split.
Buyers voluntarily pay taxes for sellers
The demand curve shifts right by the tax amount
The tax creates a price ceiling
q.commonError: confuses_who_remits_tax_with_who_bears_tax
q.feedback: Legal remittance does not determine economic burden. Prices adjust based on supply and demand elasticities.

q.q: A new production method cuts the cost of making solar panels. What happens in the solar panel market?
options: Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Demand increases, price rises, and quantity rises
Quantity demanded decreases because supply rose
q.commonError: confuses_supply_increase_with_demand_increase
q.feedback: Lower production costs increase supply, which lowers price and raises quantity.

q.q: A tax on producers raises the cost of selling bottled water. What is the likely market effect?
options: Supply decreases, price rises, and quantity falls
Supply increases, price falls, and quantity rises
Demand decreases, price falls, and quantity falls
Demand increases because taxes fund public services
q.commonError: does_not_treat_tax_as_cost_increase
q.feedback: A tax on producers raises production cost, shifting supply left and reducing quantity.

q.q: Producers expect the future price of a product to rise sharply, so they hold inventory back today. What happens to current supply?
options: Current supply decreases
Current supply increases
Current demand decreases
Quantity supplied increases because current price changed
q.commonError: gets_producer_expectation_effect_backwards
q.feedback: If sellers expect higher future prices, they may reduce current supply to sell later.

q.q: Producers expect a temporary price spike next month and can store the product cheaply. What pattern is most plausible?
options: Current and future supply both rise because firms expand production immediately and store none of it.
Current supply falls as firms hold inventory, while future supply rises when the inventory is released.
Current supply rises as firms sell inventory before the expected spike, while future supply falls.
Current quantity supplied falls along one curve because the current product price decreases.
q.commonError: Applying future price expectations in the wrong time direction.
q.feedback: When storage is feasible, a higher expected future price can reduce current supply and increase supply when the stored goods are later sold.

q.q: A surge in demand raises the equilibrium price. Firms expand output, and new firms later enter the industry. Which sequence is correct?
options: First supply shifts right; later quantity supplied falls along the curve.
Both responses are movements along the original supply curve.
First quantity supplied rises along the curve; later entry shifts market supply right.
Both responses are supply shifts caused by the good’s own price.
q.commonError: Treating immediate output response and later firm entry as the same kind of change.
q.feedback: The higher price first causes a movement along supply. Entry is a nonprice determinant that later shifts market supply right.

q.q: A drought reduces crop yields, while the market price of the crop rises because demand is unchanged. What is the best description?
options: Supply shifts right because the higher equilibrium price encourages more production after the drought.
Quantity supplied falls along the original supply curve while the curve itself remains unchanged.
Demand shifts left because the drought changes buyer preferences rather than production conditions.
Supply shifts left, and the higher price causes movement upward along the new supply curve.
q.commonError: Using the higher equilibrium price as evidence of an increase in supply.
q.feedback: The drought is a supply shifter. The resulting higher price determines the quantity supplied on the new, left-shifted curve.

q.q: If demand is less elastic than supply, why do buyers bear more of a tax?
options: Buyers are less able to reduce quantity demanded when price rises
Buyers legally pay all taxes
Sellers are less able to adjust quantity supplied
Demand shifts right after the tax
q.commonError: misses_why_less_elastic_side_bears_more
q.feedback: The less elastic side adjusts less, so it bears more of the tax burden.

q.q: If supply is perfectly inelastic and demand is elastic, who bears the tax burden?
options: Sellers bear all of it.
Buyers bear all of it
No one bears it
The government bears it because supply is vertical
q.commonError: thinks_buyers_always_bear_tax_when_price_rises
q.feedback: With perfectly inelastic supply, quantity supplied cannot respond to the tax. Sellers therefore bear the entire tax burden through a lower net price received.

q.q: A tax is imposed on a good with elastic demand and highly inelastic supply. Which result is most likely?
options: Sellers bear most of the burden
Buyers bear most of the burden
Demand increases because the tax is high
The legal assignment alone determines burden
q.commonError: thinks_buyers_always_bear_consumption_taxes
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more. If supply is highly inelastic, sellers bear most of the tax.

q.q: A student says, 'The price rose after the tax, so buyers paid the entire tax.' What is the flaw?
options: Buyers bear only the increase above the old equilibrium price.
Any price increase means buyers pay everything
Sellers cannot bear taxes if buyers pay more
Tax incidence is unrelated to prices
q.commonError: confuses_price_increase_with_full_tax
q.feedback: Buyers bear the part of the tax reflected in the higher price they pay; sellers bear the part reflected in the lower price they receive.

q.q: Before tax, price is $20. After tax, buyers pay $24 and sellers receive $18. Which statement correctly splits the burden?
options: Buyers bear $4 and sellers bear $2
Buyers bear $2 and sellers bear $4
Buyers bear $6 and sellers bear $0
Buyers bear $24 and sellers bear $18
q.commonError: uses_after_tax_prices_as_burden_amounts
q.feedback: Buyers pay $4 more than before, while sellers receive $2 less than before.

q.q: A tax is imposed on a good with highly inelastic demand and elastic supply. Which policy outcome is most likely?
options: Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
Sellers bear most of the burden and quantity falls dramatically
Buyers bear no burden because sellers legally pay
The tax creates a surplus equal to the tax
q.commonError: separates_elasticity_from_quantity_response
q.feedback: Inelastic demand means buyers bear more and reduce quantity less in response to the tax.

q.q: Supply is much less elastic than demand. A tax is imposed. What is the likely result?
options: Sellers bear more of the burden because quantity supplied is less responsive
Buyers bear more of the burden because demand is more elastic
The burden must be equal because the tax wedge is fixed
The side required to remit the tax bears more because statutory payment determines the economic burden
q.commonError: assigns_burden_to_more_elastic_side
q.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If supply is less elastic than demand, sellers bear more of the burden.

q.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
q.q: If the unemployment rate falls because many jobless workers stop searching, what is the best interpretation?
options: Measured unemployment fell, but the labor market may not have improved
Employment must have increased strongly
Structural unemployment disappeared
GDP must have increased
q.feedback: A falling unemployment rate can be misleading if discouraged workers leave the labor force.

q.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
q.q: Adult population is 300 million. Labor force participation is 62%. The unemployment rate is 5%. How many people are unemployed?
options: 9.3 million
15 million
114 million
186 million
q.feedback: Labor force = 0.62 x 300 = 186M. Unemployed = 0.05 x 186 = 9.3M.

q.commonError: Dividing unemployed workers by the whole population instead of the labor force.
q.q: The unemployment rate falls from 6% to 5%, but employment also falls. What likely happened?
options: Some unemployed workers left the labor force
Labor demand must have increased
Every discouraged worker found a job
The adult population became zero
q.feedback: The unemployment rate can fall even when employment falls if enough jobless workers stop searching.

q.commonError: Counting discouraged workers as unemployed even after they stop actively searching.
q.q: A recession causes job loss, and some unemployed workers become discouraged. Why might the unemployment rate understate the recession's damage?
options: Discouraged workers are not counted as unemployed once they stop searching
Discouraged workers are counted twice
All discouraged workers are counted as employed
The unemployment rate includes only retired people
q.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, which can hide labor market weakness.

q.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
q.q: If measured unemployment falls because 1M unemployed workers become discouraged, while employment is unchanged, what happens to labor force participation?
options: It falls
It rises
It stays unchanged
It becomes equal to unemployment
q.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, so labor force participation falls.

q.commonError: Using unemployed workers instead of the labor force in the participation formula.
q.q: Adult population is 250 million, labor force participation is 64%, and unemployment is 8 million. How many people are employed?
options: 152 million
160 million
242 million
168 million
q.feedback: Labor force = 0.64 x 250 = 160 million. Employed = 160 - 8 = 152 million.

q.q: Employment rises by 100,000, unemployment rises by 50,000, and labor-force participation rises. What likely happened?
options: The labor force must have shrunk
More people entered the labor force, and not all found jobs immediately
The unemployment rate must be zero
Everyone who entered the labor force became employed
q.commonError: sees_rising_unemployment_as_always_job_destruction
q.feedback: Unemployment can rise when more people enter the labor force and some are still searching.

q.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both changes reduce cyclical unemployment, so total unemployment must fall” in this unemployment types task.
q.q: A matching platform shortens job searches, but a recession simultaneously reduces vacancies. Which prediction distinguishes the affected components without assuming their sizes?
options: Frictional falls, cyclical rises; the net change needs relative sizes.
Frictional falls, cyclical falls; improved matching offsets the recession's lost vacancies.
Frictional rises, cyclical rises; recession makes faster searches less effective by definition.
Frictional is unchanged, cyclical rises; faster searches affect participation alone.
q.feedback: Faster matching reduces normal search duration, while weaker demand creates cyclical joblessness. The net change cannot be signed without magnitudes.
